children.title: Restoration Failure Alternative
children.top_down_role: Global alternatives arising when feasibility cannot be restored.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:X\to\mathbb R_+\) be the violation objective used by restoration, and let \(\{x_{r,j}\}\) be restoration iterates produced from a normal-phase iterate. Let \(\chi_h(x)\) be a first-order criticality measure for \(\min_{x\in X}h(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global alternative for a restoration phase that cannot return an acceptably feasible and compatible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration phase terminates with the restoration-failure alternative if it produces a limit point \(\bar x\) satisfying \[x_{r,j}\to\bar x,\qquad h(\bar x)>0,\qquad \chi_h(\bar x)=0,\] and cannot produce a point that is both acceptable to the current filter and compatible with the normal step-generation subproblem. Thus \(\bar x\) is an infeasible first-order stationary point of the restoration problem \(\min h(x)\), often interpreted as a point of locally least infeasibility. This alternative is distinct from numerical failure: it is a mathematically specified stationary outcome for the chosen violation measure. It also differs from a certificate that the original constraints are globally infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration failure occurs when the restoration sequence converges to a point with positive constraint violation that is first-order stationary for minimizing the chosen violation measure, and restoration cannot return an acceptable compatible point to the normal algorithm. The result identifies local least infeasibility, not global infeasibility of the original problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(\bar x)>0\) and \(\chi_h(\bar x)=0\) define the infeasible stationary restoration-failure alternative.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For differentiable unconstrained restoration, \(\chi_h(\bar x)=0\) may be written \(\nabla h(\bar x)=0\).
For nonsmooth \(h\), stationarity must use the generalized derivative adopted by the restoration solver.
special_cases_latex: If \(h(\bar x)=0\), the outcome is successful feasibility restoration rather than this alternative.
immediate_consequences_latex: The original optimization phase cannot resume through the required compatibility interface.
The point may still be diagnostically useful as a locally least-infeasible point.
boundary_notes: Stationarity of \(h\) is not a proof that no feasible point exists elsewhere.
Premature termination due to resource limits is not this mathematical alternative unless the stationarity condition is established.

notation.meaning: First-order criticality measure for the restoration objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniform Contractive Restoration Recovery
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Varying restoration contractions force feasibility whenever their cumulative product vanishes; a divergent sum of contraction deficits is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_j\) be successive restoration returns and suppose \(\theta(z_{j+1})\le\kappa_j\theta(z_j)\) with \(0\le\kappa_j<1\). Then \(\theta(z_j)\le\theta(z_0)\prod_{i=0}^{j-1}\kappa_i\). Consequently, \(\prod_{i=0}^{\infty}\kappa_i=0\) implies \(\theta(z_j)\to0\). In particular, the product vanishes if \(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}(1-\kappa_i)=\infty\).
assumptions_latex: Every indexed restoration return satisfies the displayed contraction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \prod_{i=0}^{\infty}\kappa_i=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \theta(z_j)\to0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient cumulative-contraction condition for varying restoration-return factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Contractive Restoration Returns Force Feasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Successive restoration returns with one uniform contraction factor drive violation geometrically to zero and cross any positive tolerance in logarithmically many returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_j\) be successive points returned by restoration. If one constant \(\kappa_R\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\theta(z_{j+1})\le\kappa_R\theta(z_j)\) for every \(j\), then \(\theta(z_j)\le\kappa_R^j\theta(z_0)\to0\). For \(0<\varepsilon<\theta(z_0)\), no more than \[\left\lceil\frac{\log(\theta(z_0)/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\kappa_R)}\right\rceil\] such contractions are required to obtain a returned point with violation at most \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(z_j)\le\kappa_R^j\theta(z_0)\to0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional convergence and threshold-crossing bound for successive successful restoration returns.

notation.meaning: The j-th successfully returned restoration point.

knowledge_statements.title: Successful Contractive Return May Remain Infeasible
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration point can satisfy a contraction-based recovery test while remaining infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta(x)=|x|\), enter restoration at \(x_k=1\), choose \(\kappa_R=3/4\), and return \(z=1/2\). Then \(\theta(z)=1/2\le(3/4)\theta(x_k)\), while \(\theta(z)>0\).
assumptions_latex: Any additional method-specific return tests are satisfied.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(z)\le\kappa_R\theta(x_k)\quad\text{and}\quad\theta(z)>0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-contraction recovery with positive returned violation.

notation.meaning: Point from which restoration is entered.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Recovery Need Not Produce a Feasible Point
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration may recover by returning a less infeasible point; recovery does not necessarily mean exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose restoration may return \(z\) when \(\theta(z)\le\kappa_R\theta(x_k)\) for some \(0<\kappa_R<1\), together with any other required tests. If \(\theta(x_k)>0\), this condition permits \(0<\theta(z)\le\kappa_R\theta(x_k)\). Thus recovery under a finite-contraction rule is a sufficient-progress outcome, not a certificate of exact feasibility. Exact feasibility follows only if the return rule separately requires \(\theta(z)=0\).
assumptions_latex: The considered return rule permits finite contraction rather than requiring zero violation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(z)\le\kappa_R\theta(x_k)\not\Rightarrow\theta(z)=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interpretation of recovery rules based on finite contraction of constraint violation.

notation.meaning: Point from which restoration was entered.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Recovery Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Condition permitting a failed main iteration to return from restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\) be the point from which restoration was entered, let \(z\) be a restoration trial point, and fix \(0<\kappa_R<1\). Restoration achieves recovery when \[\theta(z)\le\kappa_R\theta(x_k)\] and \((\theta(z),f(z))\) is acceptable to every entry of the current main filter under its prescribed margins. The method may then set \(x_{k+1}=z\), update the filter consistently, and resume the main SQP or interior-point iteration. If either the required feasibility reduction or filter acceptability fails, this recovery alternative has not occurred.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration recovers when it produces a sufficiently less infeasible point that is also acceptable to the main filter.
assumptions_latex: \(\theta:X\to\mathbb R_+\) is the restoration violation measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(z)\le\kappa_R\theta(x_k)\) together with filter acceptability permits return to the main iteration at \(z\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the recovery-alternative leaf. The proposed feasibility reduction and filter-acceptability test is coherent, but the exact reduction factor, permission to return to the main iteration, and archive update are method-specific and unsupported by a citation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditional convergence consequence for a sequence of successful restoration returns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_j\) be successive points returned by restoration and suppose a common constant \(\kappa_R\in(0,1)\) satisfies \(\theta(z_{j+1})\le\kappa_R\theta(z_j)\) for every \(j\). Then \(\theta(z_j)\le\kappa_R^j\theta(z_0)\to0\). Moreover, if \(\theta(z_0)>\varepsilon>0\), at most \[\left\lceil\frac{\log(\theta(z_0)/\varepsilon)}{\log(1/\kappa_R)}\right\rceil\] such contractions can occur while the returned violation remains greater than \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated restoration returns with one uniform multiplicative contraction factor drive violation geometrically to zero and admit a logarithmic threshold-crossing bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(z_j)\le\kappa_R^j\theta(z_0)\to0.

notation.meaning: The j-th point successfully returned from restoration.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniformly Contractive Recoveries Force Feasibility
Positive Violation Stationarity Does Not Imply Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible constraint system can have a positive-violation stationary point of its least-squares restoration objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c(x)=x^2-1\) and \(v(x)=\tfrac12c(x)^2\). Then \(c(0)=-1\neq0\) and \(v'(0)=c'(0)c(0)=0\), so \(x=0\) is stationary at positive constraint violation. Nevertheless, \(c(1)=c(-1)=0\), so the original equality constraint is feasible.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary on interpreting restoration stationarity as an infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Stationary Constraint-Violation Alternative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order certificate for restoration stationarity at positive infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For equality residual \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), define the restoration objective \(v(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|_2^2\). Since \(\nabla v(x)=J(x)^\mathsf Tc(x)\), a point \(z\) satisfying \[\|c(z)\|_2>0,\qquad J(z)^\mathsf Tc(z)=0\] is a stationary point of the constraint-violation problem with positive violation. Numerically, the verifiable approximate certificate is \(\|c(z)\|_2\ge\varepsilon_v\) and \(\|J(z)^\mathsf Tc(z)\|_2\le\varepsilon_s\) for declared tolerances \(\varepsilon_v>0\) and \(\varepsilon_s\ge0\). This certificate does not alone establish that the original constraints are infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive residual together with a zero violation gradient certifies stationary constraint violation, but not global infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(z)\ne0\) and \(J(z)^\mathsf Tc(z)=0\) certify positive stationary constraint violation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind correctly matches the terminal container, and the least-squares stationarity identity and warning about infeasibility are precise. A source is still required to establish that this certificate is the intended restoration-failure alternative in filter methods and to support the numerical termination convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Global Violation Lower Bound Certifies Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A verified positive global lower bound on an exact violation function certifies infeasibility; a positive value at one restoration point does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v:X\to\mathbb R_+\) satisfy \(v(x)=0\) if and only if \(x\) is feasible. If a verified bound \(v(x)\ge\delta>0\) holds for every \(x\in X\), then the constraint system is infeasible. Conversely, any feasible \(\bar x\in X\) implies \(\inf_{x\in X}v(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall x\in X,\ v(x)\ge\delta>0\bigr]\Longrightarrow\{x\in X:v(x)=0\}=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate separating local restoration failure from global infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility Need Not Give a Positive Violation Infimum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An infeasible system can have violation values approaching zero, so infeasibility need not admit a positive violation lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(X=\mathbb R\), let \(c(x)=e^{-x}\) and \(v(x)=|c(x)|=e^{-x}\). No finite \(x\) satisfies \(c(x)=0\), but \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}v(x)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in\mathbb R:c(x)=0\}=\varnothing,\qquad \inf_{x\in\mathbb R}v(x)=0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positive global violation lower bound is sufficient but not necessary for infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Restoration Stationarity Can Coexist with Feasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex squared-residual restoration objective may have a positive stationary point although the constraints are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c(x)=x^3-3x\) and \(v(x)=\tfrac12c(x)^2\). The constraint is feasible at \(x\in\{0,\pm\sqrt3\}\). At \(z=1\), \(c(1)=-2\), \(v(1)=2>0\), and \(v'(1)=c(1)c'(1)=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: v(1)>0,\qquad v'(1)=0,\qquad \{x:c(x)=0\}\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonconvex boundary showing that local restoration stationarity does not certify infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Restoration Stationarity Can Certify Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex exact violation function, a zero-gradient point with positive violation supplies a positive global lower bound and certifies infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(v:X\to\mathbb R_+\) be a convex exact violation function, meaning \(v(x)=0\) exactly at feasible points. If \(v\) is differentiable at \(z\in X\), \(\nabla v(z)=0\), and \(v(z)>0\), then \(z\) globally minimizes \(v\) on \(X\), so \(v(x)\ge v(z)>0\) for every \(x\in X\) and the constraint system is infeasible on \(X\).
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is convex on \(X\) and differentiable at \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf_{x\in X}v(x)=v(z)>0\;\Longrightarrow\;\{x\in X:v(x)=0\}=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient regime in which positive stationary violation yields a global infeasibility certificate.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Infeasibility Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary positive violation is insufficient to certify global infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the scalar equality constraint \(c(x)=x^2-1=0\) and restoration objective \(v(x)=\tfrac12c(x)^2\). At \(x=0\), \[c(0)=-1,\qquad v(0)=\tfrac12,\qquad v'(0)=c(0)c'(0)=0.\] Thus \(x=0\) is a positive-violation stationary point of restoration, yet the original constraint is feasible at \(x=1\) and \(x=-1\). Consequently, a restoration termination test based only on \(v(z)>0\) and \(\nabla v(z)=0\) cannot certify infeasibility. Such a conclusion requires additional global information, for example a verified positive lower bound on \(\inf_x v(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration can stop at positive stationary violation even when feasible points exist; global lower-bound information is needed to certify infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(z)>0\) and \(\nabla v(z)=0\) do not imply \(\{x:c(x)=0\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Scalar equality residual in the counterexample.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind is exactly appropriate, and the scalar counterexample is internally valid and directly checkable. No source is supplied, however, for its placement as a filter-restoration boundary or for the broader assertion about what additional global information constitutes an infeasibility certificate.

children.title: Eventual Filter Inactivity
children.top_down_role: Near-solution regimes in which filter restrictions cease to obstruct local steps.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Convergence Does Not Alone Imply Filter Inactivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trials can approach feasibility while a feasible archive entry continues to reject them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose acceptability relative to an archived pair \((\theta_i,\phi_i)\) requires \(\theta\le(1-\gamma_\theta)\theta_i\) or \(\phi\le\phi_i-\gamma_\phi\theta_i\), where \(\gamma_\theta,\gamma_\phi>0\). If the archive retains \((\theta_i,\phi_i)=(0,\phi_*)\) and trials satisfy \(\theta_k>0\), \(\theta_k\to0\), and \(\phi_k=\phi_*+1/k\), neither branch holds. Thus \(\theta_k\to0\) alone does not imply eventual archive acceptability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_k\to0\) alone does not imply eventual acceptability to every archived entry.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the inference from vanishing violation to eventual archive acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Archive Inactivity Versus Complete-Globalization Inactivity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eventually passing every archive entry is weaker than eventual acceptance by the whole globalization mechanism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For trials \(x_k^+\) and archives \(\mathcal F_k\), the archive is eventually inactive along the trials if some \(K\) satisfies: for every \(k\ge K\), \(x_k^+\) is acceptable relative to every entry of \(\mathcal F_k\). The complete globalization is eventually inactive only if every other required switching, model-agreement, trust-region, line-search, and correction test also accepts all sufficiently late trials. Hence complete-globalization inactivity implies archive inactivity, but the converse need not hold.
assumptions_latex: The archive predicate and every additional acceptance predicate are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{complete-globalization inactivity}\Rightarrow\text{archive inactivity}\), but not conversely in general.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantified distinction between passing the archive and passing every acceptance safeguard.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Slack Persistence for a Fixed Filter Archive
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict acceptance slack at the limiting pair persists locally, so a fixed finite archive eventually stops rejecting the trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite archive \(\mathcal F=\{(\theta_i,\phi_i)\}_{i=1}^m\). Declare \((\theta,\phi)\) acceptable when, for every \(i\), \(\theta\le(1-\gamma_\theta)\theta_i\) or \(\phi\le\phi_i-\gamma_\phi\theta_i\), where \(\gamma_\theta,\gamma_\phi>0\). If \((\theta_k,\phi_k)\to(\theta_*,\phi_*)\) and, for every archive entry, at least one branch holds strictly at \((\theta_*,\phi_*)\), then all sufficiently late pairs are acceptable to \(\mathcal F\).
assumptions_latex: For each archive entry, at least one acceptance branch holds with strict slack at the limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists K\ \forall k\ge K:\ (\theta_k,\phi_k)\text{ is acceptable to every entry of }\mathcal F.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for eventual archive inactivity under a fixed finite two-branch filter.

notation.meaning: Filter margins for the feasibility and objective branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform-Slack Inactivity for Changing Filter Archives
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform strict acceptance margin over all future retained entries makes changing filter archives eventually inactive along the convergent trials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each finite archive be \(\mathcal F_k=\{(\theta_{ki},\phi_{ki})\}_i\), and declare \((\theta,\phi)\) acceptable relative to entry \(i\) when \[\theta\le(1-\gamma_\theta)\theta_{ki}\quad\text{or}\quad\phi\le\phi_{ki}-\gamma_\phi\theta_{ki}.\] Suppose \((\theta_k^+,\phi_k^+)\to(\theta_*,\phi_*)\). If there are \(K_0\), \(\delta_\theta>0\), and \(\delta_\phi>0\) such that for every \(k\ge K_0\) and every entry of \(\mathcal F_k\), either \[\theta_*\le(1-\gamma_\theta)\theta_{ki}-\delta_\theta\] or \[\phi_*\le\phi_{ki}-\gamma_\phi\theta_{ki}-\delta_\phi,\] then every sufficiently late trial is acceptable to every entry of its current archive.
assumptions_latex: The displayed componentwise margins are uniform over every sufficiently late archive and all its entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists K\ \forall k\ge K:\ (\theta_k^+,\phi_k^+)\text{ is acceptable to every entry of }\mathcal F_k.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for eventual archive inactivity when the finite archive may change at every iteration.

notation.meaning: Finite filter archive used at iteration k.
Uniform strict margins for the feasibility and objective acceptance branches.

knowledge_statements.title: Eventual Filter Inactivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient separation condition making archived entries locally nonbinding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let trial pairs \((\theta_k^+,\phi_k^+)\) converge to \((0,\phi_*)\), and let the filter margin be \(0<\gamma_\theta<1\). Suppose that, from some index onward, every archived pair \((\theta_i,\phi_i)\) satisfies either \(\theta_i\ge\underline\theta>0\), or \(\theta_i=0\) and \(\phi_k^+\le\phi_i-\varepsilon\) for a fixed \(\varepsilon>0\). Because \(\theta_k^+\to0\), eventually \(\theta_k^+\le(1-\gamma_\theta)\theta_i\) for every positive-violation entry, while the objective branch accepts every zero-violation entry. Hence all sufficiently late trial pairs pass the archive test; only other local acceptance tests can reject them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If late trials approach feasibility while archived entries remain uniformly separated, the archive eventually ceases to reject those trials.
assumptions_latex: Zero-violation entries satisfy a uniform objective-separation condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists \(K\) such that every trial pair with \(k\ge K\) is acceptable to the archive.

notation.meaning: Filter coordinates of the kth trial point.
Uniform positive lower bound for archived violations.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits the leaf, and the separation argument is plausible for the intended two-branch filter test. The record does not explicitly state the complete objective-branch margin used in the argument, and the strong uniform archive-separation hypothesis is not tied to a standard local filter-convergence result.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantified distinction between passing the filter archive and passing every acceptance safeguard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For trial points \(x_k^+\) and archives \(\mathcal F_k\), the archive is eventually inactive along the trials if there exists \(K\) such that \(x_k^+\) satisfies the archive-acceptability predicate against every entry of \(\mathcal F_k\) for all \(k\ge K\). The complete globalization is eventually inactive only if, in addition, every other required switching, model-agreement, trust-region, line-search, or correction test accepts those trials for all sufficiently large \(k\). Archive inactivity therefore does not imply complete-globalization inactivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eventually passing every archive entry is weaker than eventual acceptance by the whole globalization mechanism.
assumptions_latex: The archive predicate and all additional acceptance predicates are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{complete-globalization inactivity}\Rightarrow\text{archive inactivity}\), while the converse need not hold.

notation.meaning: filter archive used at iteration k
trial point presented to the acceptance mechanism

knowledge_statements.title: Archive Inactivity Versus Globalization Inactivity

children.title: Filter Second-Order Correction Families
children.top_down_role: Higher-order correction interfaces for local filter acceptance.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Improvement Alone Does Not Ensure Filter Acceptance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A correction that improves feasibility can still be rejected by the filter or another required acceptance test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k+p_k+d_k\) be a corrected trial satisfying \(\theta(x_k+p_k+d_k)<\theta(x_k+p_k)\). This inequality alone does not imply filter acceptance: the corrected trial may still fail the required margin relative to an archived entry, an objective-oriented sufficient-decrease test, a trust-region agreement test, or a correction-size safeguard. Therefore a filter second-order correction must be retested by every acceptance condition prescribed by the method.
assumptions_latex: The method imposes at least one acceptance condition in addition to strict improvement over the uncorrected trial.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(x_k+p_k+d_k)<\theta(x_k+p_k)\not\Rightarrow\text{acceptance of }x_k+p_k+d_k.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between the local effect of a second-order correction and acceptance by the complete filter interface.

knowledge_statements.title: Jacobian Rank Loss Can Destroy a Bounded Filter Correction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inconsistent or increasingly ill-conditioned correction equation may have no correction or no uniformly quadratic-size correction, even when its residual is second order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the correction equation \(J_kd_k=-r_k\), solvability requires \(r_k\in\operatorname{range}(J_k)\). When it is solvable, the minimum-norm correction is \(d_k=-J_k^\dagger r_k\), so \(\|d_k\|\le \|J_k^\dagger\|\,\|r_k\|\). If the smallest positive singular value of \(J_k\) approaches zero, this bound is not uniform. Consequently, \(\|r_k\|=O(\|p_k\|^2)\) alone neither guarantees solvability nor implies \(\|d_k\|=O(\|p_k\|^2)\).
assumptions_latex: \(J_k\) is the Jacobian used by the selected correction variant.
\(p_k\) is the primary trial step and \(r_k\) is the residual targeted by the correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|r_k\|=O(\|p_k\|^2)\not\Rightarrow\exists d_k:\ J_kd_k=-r_k,\ \|d_k\|=O(\|p_k\|^2)\quad\text{without range compatibility and uniform conditioning}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularity boundary for trial-point normal corrections submitted to a filter acceptance interface.

notation.meaning: Constraint Jacobian used in the correction equation.
Constraint residual targeted by the correction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For equality constraints \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(A_k=Jc(x_k)\) have full row rank, and let \(p_k\) be a primary SQP step satisfying the linearized constraints. A correction is tested at the nonlinear trial \(x_k+p_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained minimum-norm correction; inequality-active-set and trust-region correction subproblems are nearby variants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A filter second-order correction is a vector \(\widehat p_k\) computed from the nonlinear residual at \(x_k+p_k\) so that \[A_k\widehat p_k+c(x_k+p_k)=0.\] The canonical minimum-norm member is \[\widehat p_k=-A_k^T(A_kA_k^T)^{-1}c(x_k+p_k).\] The corrected trial is \(x_k+p_k+widehat p_k\). It belongs to the filter correction family when it is attempted after the uncorrected full step fails an acceptance test because of nonlinear constraint violation, and the corrected trial is then submitted to the same filter and any active objective-decrease test. More general family members replace the linear equation by a bounded trust-region or least-squares correction subproblem while retaining the defining purpose of cancelling the residual omitted by the primary linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order correction evaluates the constraints at the primary trial point and computes a small correction that cancels that nonlinear residual in the original constraint Jacobian. The canonical correction is the minimum-norm solution of this linear equation. A filter method tests the corrected trial when the primary step is rejected because curvature causes excessive violation, thereby addressing the Maratos effect.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat p_k=-A_k^T(A_kA_k^T)^{-1}c(x_k+p_k)\) is the canonical minimum-norm filter second-order correction.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\widehat p_k\) is the solution of \(\min_p\tfrac12\|p\|^2\) subject to \(A_kp=-c(x_k+p_k)\).
special_cases_latex: If \(c(x_k+p_k)=0\), then \(\widehat p_k=0\).
For rank-deficient \(A_k\), a pseudoinverse or regularized correction requires separate specification.
immediate_consequences_latex: The correction targets nonlinear feasibility error rather than recomputing the primary tangential objective step.
The corrected point must still pass the globalization acceptance tests.
boundary_notes: The formula assumes equality constraints and full row rank.
A correction does not by itself establish a local superlinear or quadratic rate.

notation.meaning: Constraint Jacobian at the current iterate.

source_refs.locator: Section 15.5, discussion of the Maratos effect and correction remedy; Section 15.6, equation (15.36) and its minimum-norm characterization

knowledge_statements.title: Filter Second-Order Correction Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normal corrections applied after a rejected full SQP trial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an SQP step \(p_k\) whose full trial \(x_k+p_k\) fails filter acceptance because of nonlinear constraint curvature, compute a correction \(d_k\) from \[J(x_k+p_k)d_k=-c(x_k+p_k)\] or a regularized least-squares version. Form \(x_k^+=x_k+p_k+d_k\), require \(\|d_k\|\le\kappa\|p_k\|^2\), and retest \((\theta(x_k^+),f(x_k^+))\) against the unchanged archive and the applicable model or switching test. Accept \(x_k^+\) only if all tests pass. If the correction is too large, the linear system is unsuitable, or acceptance still fails, reject the corrected trial and globalize by shortening the step, contracting the trust region, or entering restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order correction reduces nonlinear constraint residual after a rejected SQP trial, but the corrected point must pass the original acceptance tests.
assumptions_latex: The primary SQP step satisfies \(\|p_k\|\) sufficiently small for a local correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corrected point is accepted only when \(\|d_k\|=O(\|p_k\|^2)\) and all filter and local model tests hold.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the second-order-correction family leaf. The correction equation, evaluation point for the Jacobian, quadratic-size safeguard, unchanged-archive rule, and fallback behavior vary among filter-SQP methods and require a method-specific citation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Order of an Exact Second-Order Correction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic local equality-residual estimate for an exact trial-point Newton correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(c\in C^2\), \(c(x_k)+J(x_k)p_k=0\), and \(J(x_k+p_k)\) has a uniformly bounded right inverse, an exact solution of \(J(x_k+p_k)d_k=-c(x_k+p_k)\) satisfies \(d_k=O(\|p_k\|^2)\) and \(c(x_k+p_k+d_k)=O(\|p_k\|^4)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact trial-point Newton correction can reduce a second-order equality residual to fourth order.
assumptions_latex: The chosen right inverses of \(J(x_k+p_k)\) are uniformly bounded.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Order of an Exact Second-Order Correction

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns the interface between higher-order corrections and filter acceptance. The accepted record supplies the locally essential retesting boundary. General residual-order geometry is deferred and cross-indexed to Curved-Constraint Corrections; stationary limits, restoration outcomes, and eventual inactivity remain sibling scopes.

children.title: Filter Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Archive, stagnation, and phase-transition limitations of filter globalization.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Operational Failure Boundary of Filter Globalization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_k\) be the archive, \(h_k\) the violation, \(\alpha_k\) a line-search step length or \(\Delta_k\) a trust-region radius, and \(q_k\in\{N,R\}\) the normal/restoration phase.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational boundary taxonomy for archive pressure, acceptance stagnation, and unsuccessful phase transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The filter failure boundary is the set of run states satisfying at least one of the following predicates: \[B_{\mathrm{stall}}:\ \inf_{j\ge k}\alpha_j=0\quad\text{or}\quad\inf_{j\ge k}\Delta_j=0\] along rejected trials without convergence; \[B_{\mathrm{rest}}:\ h(\bar x)>0,\quad\chi_h(\bar x)=0\] for a terminal restoration limit; or \[B_{\mathrm{archive}}(M):\ |\mathcal F_k|>M\] for a prescribed storage or comparison budget \(M\). A phase-cycling boundary may additionally be declared when normal and restoration phases alternate infinitely often while neither \(h_k\to0\) nor a stationarity measure tends to zero. These predicates define limitations requiring safeguards; they do not assert that every conforming filter algorithm reaches them.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A filter method reaches an operational failure boundary when rejected trials force step control toward zero without convergence, restoration terminates at a positively infeasible stationary point, or the nondominated archive exceeds a declared resource budget. Repeated normal-restoration alternation without limiting feasibility or stationarity is a related boundary. The predicates classify failure modes rather than claiming they inevitably occur.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_{\mathrm{stall}}\cup B_{\mathrm{rest}}\cup B_{\mathrm{archive}}(M)\), optionally augmented by a phase-cycling predicate, defines the stated operational failure boundary.
special_cases_latex: A line-search safeguard \(\alpha<\alpha_{\min}\) detects impending line-search stagnation and transfers control to restoration.
Trust-region incompatibility after repeated contraction is an analogous phase-transition trigger.
immediate_consequences_latex: A robust implementation must specify behavior at each declared boundary.
Restoration failure is mathematically different from archive resource exhaustion.
boundary_notes: The archive-budget predicate depends on an external implementation budget and is not an intrinsic mathematical failure.
The inspected sources support stagnation and restoration alternatives, but not one canonical combined failure-boundary definition.

children.title: Filter Archive Growth
children.top_down_role: Implementation pressure from numerous nondominated entries.

knowledge_statements.title: Filter Archive Growth
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A two-coordinate filter can contain arbitrarily many nondominated entries, causing linear storage and linear-time direct acceptance checks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For minimization in both filter coordinates, an archive retains points that are mutually nondominated. For any \(m\ge1\), the pairs \[z_i=\left(\frac{i}{m+1},1-\frac{i}{m+1}\right),\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,\] are mutually nondominated because improving the first coordinate worsens the second. Thus no dimension-independent finite bound on archive cardinality follows from nondominance alone. An explicit archive of size \(m\) requires \(\Theta(m)\) pair storage, and a direct acceptability test comparing a trial with every entry costs \(\Theta(m)\) coordinate comparisons in the worst case. Pruning, aggregation, discretization, or specialized search structures are therefore needed for stronger operational bounds.
assumptions_latex: The archive stores every mutually nondominated pair without aggregation or a size cap.
Acceptance is checked by direct comparison against all stored entries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal F|\) is unbounded under nondominance alone, with direct storage and query costs \(\Theta(|\mathcal F|)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case storage and comparison cost without archive-size safeguards.

notation.meaning: A pair in an arbitrary finite nondominated family.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound kind fits the archive-growth leaf. The nondominated construction is correct, and linear storage and worst-case direct-scan cost follow under the stated explicit unsorted-archive model. A source is nevertheless absent for the filter-archive context and operational complexity model.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Filter Archive Growth and Budget Exceedance
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_k\) be the finite nondominated archive after iteration \(k\), let \(N_k=|\mathcal F_k|\), and let \(M\in\mathbb N\) be an implementation budget for stored pairs or pairwise acceptance comparisons.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative definition of archive-size growth; the supplied sources do not give a canonical complexity or storage threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A filter run exhibits archive growth on an index set \(K\subseteq\mathbb N\) when \(N_{k+1}>N_k\) for every \(k\in K\). Growth is unbounded when \[\sup_{k\ge0}N_k=\infty,\] and it creates archive pressure relative to budget \(M\) at the first index \[\tau_M=\inf\{k:N_k>M\}.\] Because each successful insertion may delete dominated pairs, \(N_k\) need not be monotone. A cumulative-growth measure is therefore \[G_K=\sum_{k\in K}\max\{0,N_{k+1}-N_k\}.\] These definitions concern the number of retained nondominated entries, not the number of all previously evaluated trial points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Archive growth means that insertion increases the number of retained nondominated pairs. It is unbounded if archive sizes have no finite uniform bound, and it exceeds an implementation budget at the first iteration whose size is larger than that budget. Since pruning can later reduce the archive, cumulative positive growth is distinct from current size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_k=|\mathcal F_k|\), \(\sup_kN_k=\infty\), and \(\tau_M=\inf\{k:N_k>M\}\) define archive growth, unbounded growth, and budget exceedance.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Unbounded growth is equivalent to \(\forall M\in\mathbb N\ \exists k:\ |\mathcal F_k|>M\).
special_cases_latex: If every insertion deletes at least one old pair, then \(N_{k+1}\le N_k\) at those iterations.
An empty initial archive has \(N_0=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A direct acceptance scan costs a number of pair comparisons proportional to \(N_k\).
Pruning can keep current size bounded even when cumulative insertions are unbounded.
boundary_notes: No inspected authoritative source supplies a canonical archive-growth complexity theorem or prescribed budget.
Geometric indexing structures may change comparison cost without changing \(N_k\).
review_flags: The mathematical size predicates are explicit, but no inspected source supports them as a canonical named filter-archive growth definition.
A source addressing archive size, storage, or comparison complexity is required.
knowledge_statements.title: Filter Archive Growth and Budget Exceedance

children.title: Near-Feasible Filter Stagnation
children.top_down_role: Weak progress when infeasibility is small but persistent.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Window Near-Feasible Stagnation Diagnostic
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Small positive violation, nonstationarity, and negligible best trial progress over a finite window provide a stagnation warning, not a convergence or infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(W\ge1\) and positive thresholds \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}},\underline\theta,\underline\chi,\varepsilon_p\). For \(i=k-W+1,\ldots,k\), let \(Y_i\) be the finite nonempty trial set and define \[P_i=\max\left\{\max_{y\in Y_i}[\theta(x_i)-\theta(y)]_+,\ \max_{y\in Y_i}[f(x_i)-f(y)]_+\right\}.\] Report suspected near-feasible filter stagnation when \(\underline\theta\le\theta(x_i)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}\), \(\chi(x_i)\ge\underline\chi\), and \(P_i\le\varepsilon_p\) throughout the window. This event neither proves asymptotic stagnation nor certifies optimality, feasibility, or infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(f\), \(\theta\), and \(\chi\) are finite on tested iterates and trials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall i\in\{k-W+1,\ldots,k\}:\underline\theta\le\theta(x_i)\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}},\ \chi(x_i)\ge\underline\chi,\ P_i\le\varepsilon_p\right]\Longrightarrow\text{report suspected stagnation}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational warning test approximating the accepted asymptotic pathology without asserting infinite stagnation.

notation.meaning: Best generated feasibility or objective improvement at iteration i.

knowledge_statements.title: Concrete Near-Feasible Nonstationary Filter Stagnation Pattern
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact small residual and nonzero objective gradient can persist while generated improvements vanish and eventually fail fixed filter margins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}\), let \(c(x)=x-\varepsilon\), \(\theta(x)=|c(x)|\), \(f(x)=x\), and \(x_k=0\). Let \(Y_k=\{1/k\}\) and \(\chi(x_k)=|f'(x_k)|=1\). For sufficiently large \(k\), \(\theta(x_k)=\varepsilon\), \(\theta(1/k)=\varepsilon-1/k\), and the best generated feasibility improvement is \(1/k\to0\), while the objective improvement is zero. If the filter contains \((\varepsilon,0)\) and requires either \(\theta(y)\le(1-\gamma_\theta)\varepsilon\) or \(f(y)\le-\gamma_f\theta(y)\), every sufficiently large trial is rejected and the accepted iterate remains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(x_k)=\varepsilon>0,\qquad \chi(x_k)=1,\qquad \max_{y\in Y_k}[\theta(x_k)-\theta(y)]_+=1/k\to0.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A valid violation function and fixed filter entry realize persistent small positive violation, nonstationarity, and vanishing generated progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Near-Feasible Filter Stagnation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near-feasible stagnation is persistent small positive violation away from declared stationarity while the best generated feasibility and objective improvements vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a declared near-feasibility threshold \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}>0\). Let \(x_k\) be accepted iterates, let \(Y_k\) be the finite nonempty set of trials generated at iteration \(k\), let \(\theta\ge0\) be the violation coordinate, and let \(\chi\ge0\) be a declared criticality measure. The run exhibits asymptotic near-feasible filter stagnation along an infinite set \(K\) if constants \(0<\underline\theta\le\overline\theta\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}\) and \(\underline\chi>0\) exist such that \(\underline\theta\le\theta(x_k)\le\overline\theta\) and \(\chi(x_k)\ge\underline\chi\) for \(k\in K\), while \[\max_{y\in Y_k}[\theta(x_k)-\theta(y)]_+\to0,\qquad \max_{y\in Y_k}[f(x_k)-f(y)]_+\to0\quad(k\in K).\]
assumptions_latex: Each indexed iteration generates a finite nonempty trial set \(Y_k\).
\(f\), \(\theta\), and \(\chi\) are finite on the indexed iterates and trials.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The run has persistent near-feasible, nonstationary, vanishing-progress behavior along }K.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Observable asymptotic pathology distinguished from convergence to feasibility and stationary termination.

notation.meaning: Finite set of trials generated from \(x_k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Small Violation and Small Progress Do Not Alone Establish Stagnation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing steps and progress near feasibility may signal successful convergence; stagnation additionally requires persistent positive violation away from stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The conditions \(\theta(x_k)\to0\), \(\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0\), and \(f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\to0\) are compatible with ordinary convergence to a feasible stationary point. A near-feasible stagnation diagnosis must therefore additionally establish persistent positive violation and exclude declared stationarity, for example through \(\theta(x_k)\ge\underline\theta>0\) and \(\chi(x_k)\ge\underline\chi>0\) along the diagnosed subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(x_k)\to0,\ \|x_{k+1}-x_k\|\to0,\ f(x_k)-f(x_{k+1})\to0\not\Rightarrow\text{near-feasible filter stagnation}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating near-feasible stagnation from ordinary convergence to a feasible stationary point.

notation.meaning: Criticality measure used to exclude stationary convergence.

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Feasible Filter Stagnation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure pattern for a filter using objective value and scalar constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\), let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(\theta(x)=\lVert h(x)\rVert\). Near-feasible filter stagnation occurs for iterates \((x_k)\) when \(0<\theta(x_k)\leq\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}\) eventually, yet there exist \(\varepsilon_\theta,\varepsilon_f>0\) such that every generated trial point \(y_k\) satisfies \(\theta(y_k)>\theta(x_k)-\varepsilon_\theta\theta(x_k)\) and \(f(y_k)>f(x_k)-\varepsilon_f\theta(x_k)\), or is dominated by the current filter. Thus neither feasibility nor objective progress sufficient for acceptance is obtained while infeasibility persists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stagnation occurs when violation remains small but positive and every trial step fails both the required feasibility decrease and objective decrease, or is filter-dominated.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) are defined on a neighborhood containing all iterates and trial points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k)\) exhibits near-feasible filter stagnation.

notation.meaning: trial point generated from the current iterate

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes the node role through persistent small violation and failure of both filter progress tests

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, but the proposed thresholds and disjunctive filter-dominance condition are algorithm-specific and uncited. It is also unclear whether filter domination is an alternative to failure of both decrease tests or an additional condition. An authoritative filter-method locator is required to determine the correct acceptance inequalities and quantifiers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit sequence satisfying persistent small violation, nonstationarity, and vanishing best generated progress.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}\). Let \(f(x)=x\), \(\theta(x)=\varepsilon\), \(\chi(x)=|f'(x)|=1\), accepted iterates \(x_k=0\), and trial sets \(Y_k=\{1/k\}\). Then \(0<\theta(x_k)=\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_{\mathrm{nf}}\) and \(\chi(x_k)=1\), while \[\max_{y\in Y_k}[\theta(x_k)-\theta(y)]_+=0,\qquad \max_{y\in Y_k}[f(x_k)-f(y)]_+=0.\] Hence the sequence exhibits the declared near-feasible nonstationary vanishing-progress pathology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant small residual and nonzero objective gradient can coexist with trial sets offering no feasibility or objective improvement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta(x_k)=\varepsilon>0,\quad\chi(x_k)=1,\quad P_k=0\quad\text{for every }k.

notation.meaning: Best feasibility or objective improvement among generated trials.

knowledge_statements.title: Concrete Near-Feasible Nonstationary Stagnation Pattern

children.title: Filter–Restoration Cycling
children.top_down_role: Repeated phase transitions without durable feasibility or optimality progress.

knowledge_statements.title: Filter–Restoration Cycling
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cycling means infinitely repeated main-to-restoration-to-main transitions whose completed cycles deliver neither durable feasibility reduction nor objective reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) denote the main phase, \(R\) the restoration phase, and \(\theta:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+\) the violation measure. Filter–restoration cycling occurs if there are infinitely many indices \(k_j<\ell_j<k_{j+1}\) with phase transitions \(M\to R\) at \(k_j\) and \(R\to M\) at \(\ell_j\), while for some \(\delta>0\), \(\theta(x_{k_j})-\theta(x_{k_{j+1}})<\delta\) and \(f(x_{k_j})-f(x_{k_{j+1}})<\delta\) for every sufficiently large \(j\). Hence repeated restoration returns produce no durable progress of either filter coordinate.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(\theta:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}_+\) are finite at the phase-transition iterates.
The algorithm records an unambiguous phase label for each iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The execution exhibits filter–restoration cycling.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-cycling failure pattern for filter methods equipped with feasibility restoration.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: captures repeated phase transitions without lasting improvement in either filter coordinate

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the terminal container, but a fixed positive bound on each cycle's coordinate changes does not establish absence of durable progress; indefinitely many small changes may accumulate to substantial progress. A source is needed to determine whether cycling is characterized by vanishing per-cycle progress, recurrence, failure of prescribed sufficient-decrease tests, or another algorithm-specific condition.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q_k\in\{N,R\}\) label normal filter iterations and restoration iterations. Let \(h_k\ge0\) be infeasibility and \(\chi_k\ge0\) a first-order criticality measure. Fix progress tolerances \(\varepsilon_h,\varepsilon_\chi>0\) when a finite-tolerance notion is desired.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Asymptotic phase-transition failure definition; the inspected sources describe restoration triggers but do not present this cycling notion as a canonical named object.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A run exhibits filter–restoration cycling if both transition sets \[T_{NR}=\{k:q_k=N,\ q_{k+1}=R\},\qquad T_{RN}=\{k:q_k=R,\ q_{k+1}=N\}\] are infinite, while the run makes no durable feasibility or stationarity progress, expressed asymptotically by \[\liminf_{k\to\infty}h_k>0\quad\text{and}\quad\liminf_{k\to\infty}\chi_k>0.\] A finite-tolerance cycle over an interval \([a,b]\) requires at least two transitions of each type and \(h_k\ge\varepsilon_h\), \(\chi_k\ge\varepsilon_\chi\) throughout the interval. Mere repeated restoration is not cycling if \(h_k\to0\), \(\chi_k\to0\), or the process terminates at a declared restoration-failure alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Filter–restoration cycling is infinite alternation between normal and restoration phases while infeasibility and criticality remain bounded away from zero. A finite-tolerance version requires repeated transitions over a specified interval with neither progress measure dropping below its tolerance. Repeated restoration accompanied by convergence is excluded.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Infinitude of \(T_{NR}\) and \(T_{RN}\), together with positive lower limits of \(h_k\) and \(\chi_k\), defines asymptotic filter–restoration cycling.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Cycling means that neither phase becomes permanent and neither feasibility nor stationarity is approached along any subsequence.
special_cases_latex: Two successive restoration steps are structurally excluded by the cited trust-region SQP algorithm because successful restoration returns a compatible point; this does not exclude later returns to restoration.
A finite number of normal-restoration transitions is not asymptotic cycling.
immediate_consequences_latex: No subsequence satisfies both \(h_{k_j}\to0\) and \(\chi_{k_j}\to0\).
The run does not settle permanently in either algorithmic phase.
boundary_notes: The positive-liminf condition intentionally excludes productive alternation.
No inspected source supplies this exact cycling definition or a theorem establishing when it can occur.
review_flags: The exact asymptotic cycling predicate is a precise candidate construction but lacks a supporting authoritative locator.
The inspected trust-region source only supports the narrower fact that its mechanism prevents two successive restoration steps.
knowledge_statements.title: Filter–Restoration Cycling Without Durable Progress

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Repeated Complete State Certifies Deterministic Filter–Restoration Cycling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recurrence principle for a deterministic algorithmic state, proposed here for a filter-restoration execution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a deterministic implementation evolve a complete nonterminal state \(q_k=(x_k,\mathcal F_k,\pi_k,\omega_k)\). If \(q_i=q_j\) for some \(i<j\), no terminal state occurs between them, and the segment contains both an \(M\to R\) and an \(R\to M\) transition, then determinism makes the subsequent state sequence periodic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recurrence of a complete deterministic nonterminal state after both phase transitions forces periodic cycling.
assumptions_latex: \(q_k\) includes every variable affecting the next transition.
No state between \(q_i\) and \(q_j\) is terminal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: q_i=q_j\Longrightarrow q_{i+t}=q_{j+t}\quad\forall t\ge0.
knowledge_statements.title: Repeated Complete State Certifies Deterministic Filter–Restoration Cycling

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns repeated main/restoration transitions without durable feasibility or optimality progress. The immutable formalization is invalid, and the proposed exact-state certificate is deferred because its canonical home is general deterministic cycling. A filter-specific definition, protocol, diagnostic, counterexample, and anti-cycling theorem remain missing. Archive growth and within-phase stagnation are excluded to sibling leaves.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider the finite-dimensional nonlinear program \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(c_i(x)=0\) for \(i\in\mathcal E\) and \(c_i(x)\ge 0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Let \(V:X\to\mathbb R_+\) be a constraint-violation measure satisfying \(V(x)=0\) exactly at feasible points; for example, \(V(x)=\sum_{i\in\mathcal E}|c_i(x)|+\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}[c_i(x)]_-\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic nonlinear programming. The definition covers restoration as a globalization component and permits nonsmooth violation measures and approximate auxiliary solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration feasibility-management method is an iterative method with ordinary and restoration modes such that, whenever an entry predicate \(E_k\) holds at an ordinary iterate \(x_k\), it suspends the ordinary objective-oriented step and computes restoration iterates for the auxiliary problem \[\min_{x\in X}V(x).\] The restoration mode returns a point \(y_k\) only when a prescribed return predicate \(R_k(y_k)\) holds, where \(R_k\) requires both adequate feasibility improvement and compatibility with the ordinary globalization mechanism; a canonical form is \[V(y_k)\le \max\{\varepsilon_k,\rho_kV(x_k)\},\qquad 0\le\rho_k<1,\] together with filter acceptability or compatibility of the next local subproblem. It may instead terminate with a stationary-violation or failure certificate when no such return point is obtained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration feasibility-management method alternates between an ordinary optimization mode and a restoration mode. When an entry test detects failed globalization or an incompatible local subproblem, the method temporarily minimizes a nonnegative constraint-violation measure. It returns to ordinary optimization only after finding a point with prescribed violation reduction and compatibility with the ordinary acceptance mechanism; otherwise it reports a stationary-violation or failure outcome.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining state transition is \(x_k\xrightarrow{E_k}\text{restoration of }V\xrightarrow{R_k}\text{ordinary optimization}\), with restoration devoted to reducing \(V\) rather than directly minimizing \(f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The restoration phase may be described as an approximate solution of \(\min_{x\in X}V(x)\), stopped when the returned point has sufficiently small violation and is acceptable to the outer globalization device.
special_cases_latex: For a filter-SQP method, entry may occur after excessive line-search backtracking or incompatibility of a trust-region subproblem, and return requires a sufficiently small, filter-compatible violation value.
immediate_consequences_latex: Objective decrease need not be required during restoration because the restoration objective is \(V\), not \(f\).
A positive-residual stationary point of \(V\) is a legitimate distinct restoration outcome rather than a successful return point.
boundary_notes: This definition does not assert that a restoration phase always finds a feasible point.
A normal step inside every ordinary composite-step iteration is not by itself a separate restoration phase unless the method has the stated entry and return modes.

notation.meaning: Predicate that triggers restoration at iteration k.
Predicate authorizing return to ordinary optimization.

children.title: Restoration Problem Families
children.top_down_role: Auxiliary models used to reduce or diagnose constraint violation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be the domain of a constrained nonlinear program and let \(c(x)\) collect its equality and inequality residuals. At an iterate \(x_k\), let \(V_k:X\to\mathbb R_+\) be either the true violation measure or a local model of it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic restoration subproblems, including nonlinear violation minimization and local linearized or elastic models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration problem family is a collection \(\{\mathcal R_k\}\) of auxiliary problems indexed by the current iterate and algorithmic state, with \[\mathcal R_k:\qquad \min_{x\in D_k}\;V_k(x),\] where \(D_k\subseteq X\) contains the admissible restoration points, \(V_k(x)\ge0\), and \(V_k(x)=0\) signifies satisfaction of the exact constraints or of the constraint model represented by \(V_k\). The family is feasibility-oriented: its primary objective contains no required decrease term for the original objective \(f\). An approximate solution \(y_k\in D_k\) is acceptable when it satisfies a prescribed reduction or stationarity test, such as \(V_k(y_k)\le\rho_kV_k(x_k)\) with \(\rho_k<1\), or \(\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial V_k(y_k)+N_{D_k}(y_k))\le\epsilon_k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration problem family consists of auxiliary optimization problems whose objective is a nonnegative exact or modeled constraint violation. Each problem is indexed by the current iterate, has an explicitly stated admissible domain, and is solved only to a reduction or stationarity tolerance. Zero auxiliary objective represents satisfaction of the constraints encoded by that problem; the original objective is not required to decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each member has the canonical form \(\min_{x\in D_k}V_k(x)\) and is assessed by feasibility reduction or stationarity of \(V_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(V_k=V\) and \(D_k=X\), the member is direct norm-based violation minimization.
Introducing nonnegative elastic variables converts many nonsmooth norm objectives into smooth or linear constrained restoration models.
special_cases_latex: For equality constraints, \(V(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|_2^2\) gives a nonlinear least-squares restoration problem.
For mixed constraints, an \(\ell_1\) or \(\ell_\infty\) residual measure gives a nonsmooth restoration problem.
immediate_consequences_latex: A restoration problem can have a positive optimal or stationary value, so solving it need not establish feasibility.
Different norms define different restoration families even though they share the same zero set.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require global solution of the auxiliary problem.
Penalty problems that retain a material original-objective term are not pure restoration problems unless the restoration regime drops or lexicographically subordinates that term.

notation.meaning: Admissible domain of the kth restoration problem.
Normal cone to the restoration domain at x.
A suitable generalized subdifferential of the violation model.

children.title: Norm-Based Violation Minimization
children.top_down_role: Restoration models based on aggregate residual norms.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Based Violation Objective
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm-based restoration minimizes a norm of equality residuals and positive inequality violations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\), define \(r(x)=(h(x),[g(x)]_+)\) and \(\theta_p(x)=\|r(x)\|_p\), \(1\le p\le\infty\). Norm-based restoration approximately minimizes \(\theta_p\) over its safeguarded search region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Aggregate residual-norm restoration objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmoothness of Common Violation Norms
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common norm-based violation objectives are nonsmooth at points important to restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The maps \(\|r\|_1\) and \(\|r\|_\infty\) are generally nondifferentiable at zero components or tied maximal components, respectively, and \([g_i(x)]_+\) is generally nondifferentiable when \(g_i(x)=0\).
assumptions_latex: No smoothing or differentiable reformulation is imposed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta_1\text{ and }\theta_\infty\text{ need not have classical gradients}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability boundary for norm-based restoration.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Set and Norm Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All finite-dimensional residual norms have the feasible set as their zero set and are equivalent up to constants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \(\theta_p(x)=0\) iff \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\). For any \(p,q\in[1,\infty]\), constants \(a,b>0\), depending only on the residual dimension and the two norms, satisfy \(a\theta_p(x)\le\theta_q(x)\le b\theta_p(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \theta_p(x)=0\iff h(x)=0,\ g(x)\le0
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-independent properties of finite-dimensional violation measures.

knowledge_statements.title: Norm-Based Violation Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Restoration subproblem minimizing an aggregate norm of equality and inequality residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\leq0\), a norm-based violation restoration problem at \(x_k\) is \[\min_{x\in\Omega_k}\ \theta_p(x),\qquad \theta_p(x)=\left\|\bigl(h(x),[g(x)]_+\bigr)\right\|_p,\] where \([g(x)]_+\) is taken componentwise and \(\Omega_k\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) contains any restoration safeguards, bounds, or trust region. A restoration point is any computed \(x_k^R\in\Omega_k\) satisfying the prescribed approximate-minimization and feasibility-progress tests for this problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Norm-based restoration minimizes a chosen norm of equality residuals and positive inequality violations over a safeguarded restoration region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_p\) is the restoration objective and \(x_k^R\) is a norm-based restoration point.

notation.meaning: componentwise positive part of the inequality residual

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard residual-norm formulation for feasibility restoration

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind and residual-norm formulation fit the restoration-problem container, but no inspectable source is supplied. The phrase prescribed approximate-minimization and feasibility-progress tests also leaves the defining conditions for a restoration point unspecified. A restoration-specific source is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properties common to finite-dimensional norm-based violation measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r(x)=(h(x),[g(x)]_+)\in\mathbb R^{m+q}\) and \(\theta_p(x)=\|r(x)\|_p\). Then \(\theta_p(x)=0\) if and only if \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\). Moreover, for any \(p,q\in[1,\infty]\), constants \(a,b>0\), depending only on \(m+q,p,q\), satisfy \(a\theta_p(x)\le\theta_q(x)\le b\theta_p(x)\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every residual norm has exactly the feasible set as its zero set, and all finite-dimensional choices of norm are equivalent up to fixed constants.
assumptions_latex: The equality and inequality residual vector is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta_p(x)=0\iff h(x)=0,\ g(x)\le0\), and all \(\theta_p\) are uniformly equivalent.

notation.meaning: stacked equality and positive-part inequality residual

children.title: Least-Squares Restoration
children.top_down_role: Smooth squared-residual feasibility models.

knowledge_statements.title: Zero Set and Global Minimum of Least-Squares Restoration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The least-squares restoration objective is nonnegative and vanishes exactly at feasible points; when regional feasibility exists, its minimum value is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\Phi(x)=\tfrac12\|h(x)\|^2+\tfrac12\|[g(x)]_+\|^2,\] one has \(\Phi(x)\ge0\) and \[\Phi(x)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h(x)=0\ \text{and}\ g(x)\le0.\] Hence, if \(\Omega_k\) contains a feasible point, \(\min_{x\in\Omega_k}\Phi(x)=0\), and the zero-valued minimizers are exactly the feasible points in \(\Omega_k\).
assumptions_latex: For the minimum-value conclusion, \(\Omega_k\) contains a point satisfying the original constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x\in\Omega_k:\Phi(x)=0\}=\Omega_k\cap\{h=0,\ g\le0\}\), and the minimum is zero when this set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact relation between restoration feasibility and zero objective value.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient of Mixed Least-Squares Violation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared positive-part inequality violation is continuously differentiable, giving mixed least-squares restoration an explicit Jacobian-transpose residual gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\) and \(g\) are continuously differentiable, then \[\Phi(x)=\tfrac12\|h(x)\|^2+\tfrac12\|[g(x)]_+\|^2\] is continuously differentiable, including where \(g_i(x)=0\), and \[\nabla\Phi(x)=J_h(x)^\top h(x)+J_g(x)^\top[g(x)]_+.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla\Phi(x)=J_h(x)^\top h(x)+J_g(x)^\top[g(x)]_+\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth first-order representation of equality and positive-inequality squared residuals.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the inequality residual map.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Restoration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Least-squares restoration minimizes one half of the summed squared equality residuals and positive inequality violations within a restoration region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For constraints \(h(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\leq0\), the least-squares restoration objective is \[\Phi(x)=\frac12\lVert h(x)\rVert_2^2+\frac12\lVert[g(x)]_+\rVert_2^2.\] A least-squares restoration step computes an approximate minimizer of \(\Phi\) over a nonempty restoration region \(\Omega_k\). If only equality constraints are present, then \(\Phi\) is continuously differentiable whenever \(h\) is continuously differentiable, with \(\nabla\Phi(x)=J_h(x)^\mathsf{T}h(x)\).
assumptions_latex: For the gradient formula, \(h\) is continuously differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Phi\) defines the least-squares restoration model; in the equality-only case, \(\nabla\Phi(x)=J_h(x)^\mathsf{T}h(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth squared-residual restoration for equality and inequality constraints.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the equality residual map

children.title: Elastic Restoration Models
children.top_down_role: Feasibility problems using explicit constraint relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Elastic-Penalty Multiplier Bounds
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common linear elastic penalty induces box bounds on equality multipliers and upper bounds on nonnegative inequality multipliers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex elastic subproblem with equality multiplier \(\lambda\), inequality multiplier \(\mu\ge0\), and common linear elastic weight \(\rho_e>0\), finiteness of the Lagrangian infimum over \(u,v,w\ge0\) requires \[-\rho_e\mathbf1\le\lambda\le\rho_e\mathbf1,\qquad 0\le\mu\le\rho_e\mathbf1.\] Under a qualification giving strong duality, these are the multiplier bounds in the dual problem.
assumptions_latex: Strong duality is invoked only under an appropriate constraint qualification.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\lambda\|_\infty\le\rho_e\) and \(0\le\mu\le\rho_e\mathbf1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual interpretation of a convex linear-penalty elastic subproblem.

knowledge_statements.title: Slack-Elimination Equivalence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating linear-penalty elastic variables exactly yields the L1 equality and positive-inequality violation objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(x\), \[\min_{u,v,w\ge0}\ \mathbf1^\top(u+v+w)\quad\text{s.t. }h(x)-u+v=0,\quad g(x)-w\le0\] has optimal value \[\|h(x)\|_1+\|[g(x)]_+\|_1,\] attained by \(u=[h(x)]_+\), \(v=[-h(x)]_+\), and \(w=[g(x)]_+\). Thus eliminating the elastic variables yields \(\rho_e(\|h(x)\|_1+\|[g(x)]_+\|_1)+r_k(x)\).
assumptions_latex: Elastic variables are nonnegative and have an identical positive linear weight.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent nonsmooth violation model obtained by eliminating linear-penalty elastic variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Elastic Restoration Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonlinear programs with equality and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For constraints \(c(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le 0\), an elastic restoration model at \(x_k\) is
\[
\min_{x,u^+,u^-,v}\; \tfrac12\|x-x_k\|_{H_k}^2+\rho_k\mathbf 1^T(u^++u^-+v)
\]
subject to \(c(x)-u^++u^-=0\), \(g(x)-v\le0\), and \(u^+,u^-,v\ge0\), where \(H_k\succeq0\) and \(\rho_k>0\). The slacks make the restoration problem feasible whenever their required values are finite; zero optimal slacks certify satisfaction of the original constraints by the returned point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative elastic slacks relax every constraint and are penalized in the restoration objective; vanishing slacks certify restoration of the original constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) are finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The elastic model is feasible, and \(u^+=u^-=v=0\) implies \(c(x)=0\) and \(g(x)\le0\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At \(x_k\), let the local constraint model be \(a_i(d)=c_i(x_k)+\nabla c_i(x_k)^Td\). Equalities use indices \(\mathcal E\), inequalities are written as \(a_i(d)\ge0\) for \(i\in\mathcal I\), and \(D_k\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is the permitted step set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional local restoration models with explicit nonnegative relaxation variables; both weighted one-norm and shared infinity-norm elasticizations are covered.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An elastic restoration model replaces potentially inconsistent local constraints by equations or inequalities containing nonnegative relaxation variables and minimizes their weighted magnitude. Its canonical weighted \(\ell_1\) form is \[\min_{d,u,v,w}\ \sum_{i\in\mathcal E}\omega_i(u_i+v_i)+\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\omega_iw_i\] subject to \[a_i(d)+u_i-v_i=0\ (i\in\mathcal E),\qquad a_i(d)+w_i\ge0\ (i\in\mathcal I),\] \[d\in D_k,\qquad u,v,w\ge0,\qquad \omega_i>0.\] The elastic objective is zero exactly when the unrelaxed modeled constraints admit a point in \(D_k\). A shared variable \(\eta\ge0\), with \(|a_i(d)|\le\eta\) for equalities and \(a_i(d)\ge-\eta\) for inequalities, defines the corresponding weighted \(\ell_\infty\) model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An elastic restoration model makes a possibly inconsistent local constraint system feasible by adding explicit nonnegative violation variables. It minimizes a positive weighted sum, or a common maximum, of those variables. The elastic objective is zero exactly when the original unrelaxed local constraints are satisfiable within the step domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Elastic variables quantify modeled infeasibility, and their minimum weighted magnitude is the restoration objective.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Eliminating \(u,v,w\) yields minimization of \(\sum_{i\in\mathcal E}\omega_i|a_i(d)|+\sum_{i\in\mathcal I}\omega_i[a_i(d)]_-\) over \(D_k\).
The common relaxation \(\eta\) yields minimization of the maximum scaled modeled residual.
special_cases_latex: Taking \(D_k=\{d:\|d\|\le\Delta_k\}\) gives an elastic trust-region restoration model.
For affine original constraints, \(a_i(d)\) is exact rather than merely local.
immediate_consequences_latex: The elastic subproblem remains feasible whenever the step domain is nonempty and the relaxation variables are unbounded above.
A positive optimal elastic objective certifies incompatibility of the unrelaxed modeled constraints within \(D_k\), not necessarily infeasibility of the nonlinear problem.
boundary_notes: Finite upper bounds on elastic variables can destroy automatic feasibility.
A positive local elastic value is not a global infeasibility certificate for nonlinear constraints.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative elastic variables for equality and inequality residuals.
