children.title: Linearized Restoration Models
children.top_down_role: Restoration based on local linear or quadratic constraint models.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Feasibility Need Not Give Nonlinear Feasibility
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step may solve the affine restoration equation while its nonlinear trial point remains infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(c(t)=t^2-1\), at \(x=2\) the step \(d=-3/4\) satisfies \(c(2)+c'(2)d=0\), whereas \(c(2+d)=9/16\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c(x)+J(x)d=0\not\Rightarrow c(x+d)=0
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary of the affine model-feasibility test.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearized Restoration Model
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Linearized restoration seeks a safeguarded step that reduces or eliminates the affine constraint residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At x_k, a linearized equality-restoration step approximately minimizes \(\|c(x_k)+J_kd\|\) over an admissible step set \(D_k\), optionally with regularization \(\tfrac12d^TB_kd\). Exact model restoration requires \(c(x_k)+J_kd=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{d\in D_k}\left(\|c(x_k)+J_kd\|+\tfrac12d^TB_kd\right)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order equality-constraint restoration model; norm aggregation, least squares, and elastic relaxation belong to sibling leaves.

notation.meaning: constraint Jacobian at the current point

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Residual after Exact Linearized Restoration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact affine restoration step leaves a second-order nonlinear residual under a Lipschitz Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(J\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \([x,x+d]\), then \(\|c(x+d)-c(x)-J(x)d\|_2\le(L/2)\|d\|_2^2\). Hence \(c(x)+J(x)d=0\) implies \(\|c(x+d)\|_2\le(L/2)\|d\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Accuracy of an equality-restoration step satisfying the affine model.

knowledge_statements.title: Linearized Restoration Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order local restoration models for smooth finite-dimensional equality and inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(x_k\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\Delta_k>0\), define the linearized restoration model on \(\{d\in\mathbb R^n:\|d\|\le\Delta_k\}\) by
\[
M_k(d)=V\!\left(c(x_k)+J_c(x_k)d,\,[g(x_k)+J_g(x_k)d]_+\right)+\tfrac12 d^T B_k d,
\]
where \(V:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^p_+\to\mathbb R_+\) is a continuous violation measure, \([\cdot]_+\) is the componentwise positive part, and \(B_k\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric. A linearized restoration step is any global minimizer of \(M_k\) on this trust region. Such a minimizer exists because the feasible step set is nonempty and compact and \(M_k\) is continuous. The resulting step models local feasibility improvement only; nonlinear constraint violation must be evaluated separately before the trial point is accepted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linearized restoration model minimizes a continuous measure of linearized equality and inequality violation, optionally with a quadratic term, over a trust region. The model has a minimizer, but the resulting point still requires evaluation using the nonlinear constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(g:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^p\) are continuously differentiable near \(x_k\).
\(V:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^p_+\to\mathbb R_+\) is continuous and vanishes exactly when both its arguments are zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The trust-region model has at least one global minimizer \(d_k\), which represents a local linearized-feasibility step but does not by itself certify reduction of the nonlinear constraint violation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Feasibility Does Not Imply Nonlinear Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of what an exactly feasible linearized restoration model certifies.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(c(t)=t^2-1\), at \(x=2\) the step \(d=-3/4\) satisfies \(c(2)+c'(2)d=0\), but \(c(2+d)=9/16\ne0\). Hence exact feasibility of \(c(x)+J(x)d=0\) does not imply feasibility of \(x+d\) for nonlinear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A step can solve the affine restoration equations exactly while its nonlinear trial point remains infeasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(c(x)+J(x)d=0\not\Rightarrow c(x+d)=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Feasibility Does Not Imply Nonlinear Feasibility

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Accuracy of a Linearized Restoration Step
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonlinear residual remaining after a step that satisfies the affine equality model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz Jacobian on the segment \([x,x+d]\). Then \[\|c(x+d)-c(x)-J(x)d\|_2\le \frac L2\|d\|_2^2.\] Consequently, if \(c(x)+J(x)d=0\), then \(\|c(x+d)\|_2\le (L/2)\|d\|_2^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact satisfaction of the affine constraint model leaves at most a second-order nonlinear equality residual when the Jacobian is Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: \(c\) is continuously differentiable and \(J\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \([x,x+d]\).

children.title: Restoration-Phase Architecture
children.top_down_role: Structural organization of dedicated feasibility-recovery phases.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathsf O\) denote ordinary optimization mode and \(\mathsf R\) restoration mode. At iteration \(k\), the algorithm stores an iterate \(x_k\), a violation value \(V(x_k)\), and globalization state \(s_k\), such as a filter, line-search threshold, or trust-region radius.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract deterministic state-machine architecture for nonlinear-programming methods with a dedicated feasibility-recovery phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration-phase architecture is a two-mode transition system \((x_k,s_k,m_k)\), with \(m_k\in\{\mathsf O,\mathsf R\}\), satisfying: \[m_k=\mathsf O\ \wedge\ E(x_k,s_k)\Longrightarrow m_{k+1}=\mathsf R;\] while \(m_k=\mathsf R\), trial points are generated primarily to reduce a violation measure \(V\); and \[m_k=\mathsf R\ \wedge\ R(y_k,s_k)\Longrightarrow (x_{k+1},m_{k+1})=(y_k,\mathsf O).\] The entry predicate \(E\) records failure or incompatibility of the ordinary mechanism. The return predicate \(R\) requires a restoration outcome suitable for renewed optimization, normally feasibility reduction plus acceptability or local-subproblem compatibility. If neither return nor further progress is available, an escalation or terminal certificate transition is taken.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration-phase architecture is a two-mode algorithmic state machine. Ordinary optimization switches to restoration when an entry predicate detects failure or incompatibility. Restoration generates points principally to reduce constraint violation. It returns a recovered point to ordinary optimization only when a return predicate establishes sufficient feasibility and compatibility; otherwise it escalates or terminates with an outcome certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The architecture separates the transitions \(\mathsf O\to\mathsf R\), progress within \(\mathsf R\), and \(\mathsf R\to\mathsf O\), each with its own mathematical predicate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The same architecture may be represented as a finite-state machine with ordinary, restoration, escalation, success, and failure states.
special_cases_latex: In a filter line-search method, \(E\) may be \(\alpha_k<\alpha_{\min}\).
In a trust-region method, \(E\) may state that the local constrained subproblem is incompatible.
immediate_consequences_latex: Restoration acceptance need not use the same objective-decrease test as ordinary iterations.
Entry, progress, and return tolerances can be specified independently.
boundary_notes: The architecture does not prescribe one particular solver for the restoration subproblem.
A single feasibility-oriented step without a mode transition is outside this dedicated-phase definition.

children.title: Restoration Entry Regimes
children.top_down_role: Entry caused by failed globalization, inconsistent subproblems, or excessive infeasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Entry Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration begins when main globalization fails, the main subproblem is inconsistent, or current violation exceeds its allowed threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x_k\) be a main-phase iterate, \(S_k\) its main subproblem, \(\theta_k=\theta(x_k)\), and \(\theta_{\max}>0\). A restoration-entry predicate is \[E_k=F_k\lor I_k\lor V_k,\] where \(F_k\) means that the main globalization procedure produced no acceptable trial point within its prescribed finite safeguards, \(I_k\) means that \(S_k\) is infeasible or fails its consistency test, and \(V_k\) means \(\theta_k>\theta_{\max}\). Restoration is entered exactly when \(E_k\) is true; the triggering reason and current iterate are retained for the return test.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm defines finite safeguards for declaring globalization failure.
The subproblem consistency test and violation threshold are specified before evaluating \(E_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_k=\mathrm{true}\) triggers transfer from the main phase to restoration.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational predicates for transferring an iterate from the main phase to restoration.

notation.meaning: maximum violation permitted before restoration entry

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes the three entry causes named by the node role

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the entry-regime container, but asserting that restoration is entered exactly when this three-way disjunction holds defines a particular algorithm. The taxonomy role names possible causes, not a universal necessary-and-sufficient entry rule. A source must establish the predicates, safeguards, and exact trigger semantics.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an ordinary iteration \(k\), let \(\alpha_k\) be a line-search step length, \(\Delta_k\) a trust-region radius, \(Q_k\) the local step-generation problem, and \(V(x_k)\) the current constraint violation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic entry rules for line-search, trust-region, and local-model nonlinear-programming methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration entry regime is a specified predicate \(E_k\) whose truth causes an ordinary iteration to enter restoration. The canonical regime is the disjunction \[E_k=E_k^{\mathrm{LS}}\vee E_k^{\mathrm{INC}}\vee E_k^{\mathrm{V}},\] where \[E_k^{\mathrm{LS}}:\ \alpha_k<\alpha_{\min},\qquad E_k^{\mathrm{INC}}:\ Q_k\text{ is infeasible or fails its compatibility test},\] and an optional excessive-violation trigger has the form \[E_k^{\mathrm V}:\ V(x_k)>\tau_k.\] Here \(\alpha_{\min}>0\) and \(\tau_k\ge0\) are declared algorithmic thresholds. Entry records the triggering condition and initializes restoration from \(x_k\); it does not itself declare the nonlinear constraints infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration entry regime is an explicit predicate that switches an ordinary iteration into restoration. Standard triggers are a line-search step length below a fixed threshold, infeasibility or incompatibility of the current local subproblem, and optionally violation above a declared tolerance. Triggering restoration is a control decision, not an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Restoration begins exactly when the declared predicate \(E_k\) is true; otherwise the ordinary globalization mechanism remains active.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Repeated trial rejection may be encoded through a rejection counter \(j_k\ge j_{\max}\) instead of an explicit radius or step-length threshold.
special_cases_latex: For filter line search, \(E_k^{\mathrm{LS}}\) is triggered when backtracking produces \(\alpha_k<\alpha_{\min}\).
For trust-region filter SQP, incompatibility includes absence of a feasible linearized step within the trust region or insufficient room for a tangential step.
immediate_consequences_latex: Different triggers may share the same restoration subproblem while producing different diagnostic entry labels.
The method can distinguish globalization failure from modeled-constraint incompatibility.
boundary_notes: Small step length alone does not prove local infeasibility.
The optional excessive-violation trigger must be specified by the algorithm; it is not universal.

notation.meaning: Minimum accepted line-search scale before restoration entry.

children.title: Restoration Progress Globalization
children.top_down_role: Acceptance families devoted to feasibility improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Restoration-Envelope Acceptance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite-memory rule permits an increase relative to the current violation while requiring quantitative decrease below the recent violation envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R_+\), choose \(q\geq1\), and define \(M_j=\max_{\max\{0,j-q+1\}\leq i\leq j}\theta(x_i^R)\). Given a trial point \(y_j\), a declared predicted feasibility decrease \(\Delta_j>0\), and \(\sigma\in(0,1)\), accept \(y_j\) when \[\theta(y_j)\leq M_j-\sigma\Delta_j.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(y_j)<M_j\) for every accepted trial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-memory feasibility acceptance distinct from ratio-based trust-region and Armijo line-search rules.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonincrease Alone Does Not Ensure Restoration Progress
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rule requiring only nonincrease can accept an infinite constant-violation sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\theta(x)=1\) at every generated point and accept whenever \(\theta(x_{j+1}^R)\leq\theta(x_j^R)\). Every trial is acceptable although \(\theta(x_j^R)=1\) for all \(j\). Thus nonincrease alone implies neither convergence to feasibility nor strict restoration progress.
assumptions_latex: The acceptance test imposes no strict or quantitative decrease.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\theta(x_{j+1}^R)\leq\theta(x_j^R)\ \forall j\not\Rightarrow\theta(x_j^R)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for acceptance rules lacking strict or quantitative feasibility decrease.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Progress Globalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-only acceptance and radius control during restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(x)\ge0\) be the restoration merit function. From \(x_j\), a model \(m_j(s)\), and radius \(\Delta_j\), compute a trial step \(s_j\) with \(\|s_j\|\le\Delta_j\) and predicted reduction \(\operatorname{pred}_j=m_j(0)-m_j(s_j)>0\). Evaluate \(\operatorname{ared}_j=v(x_j)-v(x_j+s_j)\) and \(r_j=\operatorname{ared}_j/\operatorname{pred}_j\). Accept the trial when \(r_j\ge\eta\), where \(0<\eta<1\); otherwise retain \(x_j\). Update \(\Delta_j\) by a prescribed trust-region rule, shrinking it after rejection. Terminate this globalization loop upon satisfying a return condition or a restoration-failure condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globalize restoration by comparing actual and predicted feasibility reduction, accepting sufficiently accurate trials and shrinking the radius after rejection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted restoration trial satisfies \(v(x_j+s_j)<v(x_j)\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: During restoration let \(z_j\in X\) be the current restoration iterate, \(p_j\) a trial step, \(V\ge0\) the violation objective, and \(m_j^V\) a local model with predicted reduction \(\operatorname{pred}_j=m_j^V(0)-m_j^V(p_j)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic feasibility-oriented line-search, trust-region, or filter acceptance during a restoration phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration progress globalization rule accepts a trial point \(z_j^+=z_j+p_j\) only through a feasibility-oriented sufficient-progress condition. Canonical forms are \[V(z_j^+)\le V(z_j)-\eta\operatorname{pred}_j,\qquad \eta\in(0,1),\ \operatorname{pred}_j>0,\] or the ratio test \[\rho_j^V=\frac{V(z_j)-V(z_j^+)}{\operatorname{pred}_j}\ge\eta.\] In a filter-coupled implementation, the accepted point must additionally satisfy a margin condition against stored pairs, such as \[V(z_j^+)\le(1-\gamma)V_i\quad\text{or}\quad f(z_j^+)\le f_i-\gamma V_i\] for every relevant filter entry \((V_i,f_i)\). Rejected trials cause a reduction of step length or trust-region radius and do not replace the current restoration iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration progress is globalized by accepting a trial point only when its actual reduction in constraint violation is a prescribed fraction of predicted reduction. A filter-coupled variant also requires sufficient separation from stored violation-objective pairs. Rejected trials shrink the step scale and leave the current restoration point unchanged.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every accepted nonterminal restoration trial satisfies a quantitative decrease or filter-margin condition centered on feasibility progress.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a line search, sufficient progress may be written \(V(z_j+\alpha_jd_j)\le V(z_j)-\sigma\alpha_j\delta_j\) with \(\delta_j>0\).
For a trust region, the same rule is expressed by the actual-to-predicted reduction ratio \(\rho_j^V\).
special_cases_latex: Pure violation minimization omits the filter objective condition and uses only the reduction test for \(V\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The original objective may increase at an accepted restoration step.
Repeated rejection causes globalization contraction rather than acceptance without demonstrated feasibility progress.
boundary_notes: This definition does not require monotone violation across separately accepted ordinary-mode iterations.
A filter point acceptable solely through objective improvement may be unsuitable as a restoration-progress step unless the algorithm explicitly permits that branch.

notation.meaning: Predicted decrease in the restoration model.

children.title: Restoration Return Regimes
children.top_down_role: Transitions from feasibility recovery back to the main optimization phase.

knowledge_statements.title: Main-Phase Re-entry Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Re-entry requires recovery, globalization admissibility, and model reconstructability, but does not certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A candidate x^R is certified for main-phase re-entry when its selected recovery predicate holds, it is admissible for the active main-globalization mechanism, and the data required to construct the main model exist and satisfy the declared validity tests. This authorizes x^+=x^R only; KKT termination requires separate feasibility, stationarity, dual-feasibility, and complementarity tests as applicable.
assumptions_latex: The main phase declares its admissibility and model-validity tests.
Return and optimization termination are separate statuses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\rm ret}(x^R)\Rightarrow x^+=x^R,\qquad C_{\rm ret}(x^R)\not\Rightarrow C_{\rm KKT}(x^R).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient transition certificate distinct from optimization termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Return Predicate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A return regime is the explicit predicate authorizing transfer from restoration to the main phase and identifying the transferred primal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration return regime is a Boolean predicate \(R(x^E,x^R,s^R)\) on the restoration-entry point \(x^E\), current restoration point \(x^R\), and method-specific restoration state \(s^R\). If \(R(x^E,x^R,s^R)\) is true, control transfers to the main phase with primal starting point \(x^+=x^R\); otherwise restoration does not return at that state.
assumptions_latex: The method defines the restoration state \(s^R\) and an unambiguous Boolean predicate \(R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R(x^E,x^R,s^R)=\mathrm{true}\Rightarrow x^+=x^R\text{ and control returns to the main phase}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract transition interface without selecting an algorithm-specific feasibility threshold.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Return Is Not an Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing a feasibility-only restoration-return test does not establish stationarity or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x (x-1)^2\) subject to the identically satisfied constraint \(h(x)=0\). Its violation measure is \(\theta(x)=0\) for every \(x\), so every violation-only return test accepts \(x=0\), although \(\nabla f(0)=-2\neq0\).
assumptions_latex: The return predicate uses only constraint-violation information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R=\mathrm{true}\not\Rightarrow\text{KKT stationarity}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between successful feasibility recovery and nonlinear-program termination.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Restoration Return Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return policies combine relative or absolute feasibility recovery with any required globalization and model-reconstruction safeguards.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Common return predicates include relative recovery R_{\rm rel}:\theta(x^R)\le\kappa_R\theta(x^E), absolute recovery R_{\rm abs}:\theta(x^R)\le\varepsilon_R, main-globalization compatibility R_{\rm glob}, and reconstruction validity R_{\rm mod}. A method may combine alternative recovery tests with conjunctive safeguards, for example (R_{\rm rel}\lor R_{\rm abs})\land R_{\rm glob}\land R_{\rm mod}.
assumptions_latex: \theta is the declared nonnegative violation measure.
Individual methods explicitly state which safeguards are required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R=(R_{\rm rel}\lor R_{\rm abs})\land R_{\rm glob}\land R_{\rm mod}\quad\text{is a parameterized return-policy form}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parameterized predicates governing transfer back to the main phase.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Return Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Predicates permitting transfer from restoration back to the main optimization phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^E\) be the restoration-entry point and \(x_j^R\) a restoration iterate. For constants \(\kappa_R\in(0,1)\) and \(\theta_{\mathrm{ret}}\geq0\), define \[Q_j=\bigl[\theta(x_j^R)\leq\kappa_R\theta(x^E)\bigr]\lor\bigl[\theta(x_j^R)\leq\theta_{\mathrm{ret}}\bigr].\] A restoration return is allowed only if \(Q_j\) holds and the main-phase model or subproblem can be constructed consistently at \(x_j^R\). On return, set the new main iterate to \(x^+=x_j^R\); otherwise continue restoration or invoke its escalation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Return to the main phase after sufficient relative or absolute feasibility recovery, provided a consistent main-phase subproblem can be rebuilt.
assumptions_latex: The algorithm supplies a check for consistent construction of the main-phase model or subproblem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(Q_j\) and main-phase consistency hold, then \(x^+=x_j^R\) is a valid restoration return point.

notation.meaning: point at which restoration was entered

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: combines relative and absolute feasibility return tests with main-model consistency

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind fits the return-regime container, but the relative-or-absolute feasibility predicate and added main-subproblem consistency test constitute a particular return policy. No evidence establishes these conditions as necessary or sufficient for the intended family. An authoritative restoration architecture source is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Return Is Not an Optimality Certificate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between successful feasibility recovery and termination of the nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration return predicate depending only on constraint violation can certify feasibility recovery but cannot in general certify stationarity. For the unconstrained objective \(f(x)=(x-1)^2\) with identically zero violation \(\theta(x)=0\), every point passes every violation-only return test, whereas \(x=0\) has \(\nabla f(0)=-2\neq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Passing a feasibility-only return test does not establish optimality or KKT stationarity.
assumptions_latex: The return predicate uses only feasibility information.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: R=\mathrm{true}\not\Rightarrow \nabla f(x^R)=0\text{ or KKT stationarity}.
knowledge_statements.title: Return Is Not an Optimality Certificate

children.title: Restoration Escalation Modes
children.top_down_role: Fallback variants ranging from partial repair to dedicated feasibility solution.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal R_k^{(0)},\ldots,\mathcal R_k^{(L)}\) be restoration variants of increasing feasibility emphasis. Let \(j\) count failed trials or penalty updates within the current tier, and let \(V\) be the violation measure.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite tiered fallback systems for deterministic nonlinear-programming restoration; escalation may change tolerances, relaxation weights, domains, or the retained objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration escalation regime is an ordered family of restoration tiers together with transition predicates \[\mathcal R_k^{(0)}\prec\mathcal R_k^{(1)}\prec\cdots\prec\mathcal R_k^{(L)},\qquad F_k^{(\ell)}\Longrightarrow \ell\leftarrow\ell+1,\] where increasing \(\ell\) gives feasibility greater priority. A canonical sequence is: partial repair, obtained by stricter acceptance or a larger restoration domain; elastic repair, obtained by increasing positive weights on violation variables; and dedicated feasibility solution, obtained by dropping the original objective and solving \(\min V\). The tier-failure predicate may be \(j\ge j_{\max}^{(\ell)}\), failure to attain \(V(z^+)\le\rho_\ell V(z)\), or repeated elastic-weight updates. At the final tier, the regime must return a successful point, a stationary-violation certificate, or a declared failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration escalation regime orders several fallback variants by increasing priority given to feasibility. Failure of a quantitative progress test at one tier moves the method to the next. Typical tiers tighten or enlarge a repair step, increase elastic penalties, and finally drop the original objective to solve a dedicated violation-minimization problem. The last tier must return a recovered point or a terminal outcome.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Escalation is the monotone tier transition \(\ell\mapsto\ell+1\) triggered by a declared failure predicate, culminating in pure feasibility restoration or termination.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Repeated penalty updates followed by deletion of the original objective are an elastic-to-pure-restoration escalation.
special_cases_latex: A two-tier system consists of ordinary elastic repair followed by \(\min_{x\in X}V(x)\).
A trust-region implementation may enlarge the restoration radius before switching to a different restoration model.
immediate_consequences_latex: The escalation level records how strongly feasibility has been prioritized.
Failure of an early tier is not itself a terminal infeasibility indication.
boundary_notes: The ordering concerns feasibility emphasis, not computational cost.
An unbounded sequence of penalty increases without a terminal rule is not a complete finite escalation regime.

notation.meaning: Restoration model at escalation tier ell.

knowledge_statements.title: Soft Restoration Modes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Soft restoration tries a bounded number of feasibility-oriented steps without abandoning main-phase state, escalating if none achieves sufficient violation reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a main iterate \(x_k\), violation \(\theta\), a soft-restoration budget \(N_s\), and acceptance constant \(\eta_s\in(0,1)\). Generate at most \(N_s\) safeguarded trial steps \(d_j\) using a feasibility-oriented model while retaining the main-phase state. Accept the first step satisfying \[\theta(x_j+d_j)\leq\theta(x_j)-\eta_s\operatorname{pred}_j,\qquad \operatorname{pred}_j>0.\] Return the accepted point directly to the main phase. If no such step is found within the budget, preserve the last accepted iterate and trigger full or emergency restoration according to the escalation predicate.
assumptions_latex: Each trial step is safeguarded and has a computable predicted reduction \(\operatorname{pred}_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mode either returns a feasibility-improving point within \(N_s\) trials or triggers escalation without accepting an unsuccessful trial.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limited restoration embedded within the main phase before a full phase transfer.

notation.meaning: required fraction of predicted feasibility reduction

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: soft mode is represented as bounded feasibility work retaining main-phase state

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is plausible for a mode container, but soft-restoration semantics are implementation-specific and uncited. The statement introduces trial iterates x_j without defining their initialization or update from the input x_k, and the bounded-budget and escalation behavior cannot be validated without a source.

knowledge_statements.title: Emergency Restoration Modes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Emergency restoration solves a strongly safeguarded violation problem, accepts only verified feasibility progress, and declares failure when its finite safeguards are exhausted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input the last accepted iterate \(x_k\), violation \(\theta\), emergency region \(\Omega_k^E\), and a finite safeguard budget. Compute a safeguarded approximate solution \(z_k\in\Omega_k^E\) of \[\min_{z\in\Omega_k^E}\ \theta(z)+r_k^E(z),\] where \(r_k^E\) regularizes distance or step size. Accept \(z_k\) only if it satisfies a prescribed strict violation decrease or the restoration-return predicate. Otherwise reduce the emergency region and retry until the budget is exhausted. On exhaustion, terminate restoration with a declared feasibility failure or stationary point of the violation problem; never return an unaccepted point to the main phase.
assumptions_latex: The emergency acceptance test and finite safeguard budget are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The mode returns an accepted feasibility-improving point or a declared restoration failure, but not an unverified trial point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safeguarded fallback invoked after ordinary restoration cannot produce an acceptable step.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes emergency restoration as a safeguarded terminal fallback

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind is plausible for an emergency-mode container, but the optimization model, contraction policy, acceptance rule, and terminal behavior are uncited and algorithm-specific. Exhausting a finite budget does not by itself justify declaring a stationary point of the violation problem. A source is required to determine the valid failure and stationarity outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration Escalation Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Escalate from soft to full and then emergency restoration when finite trial budgets, model consistency, or predicted-progress tests fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_k\), \(R_k\), and \(E_k\) denote soft, full, and emergency restoration modes. With finite budgets \(N_S,N_R\), define \(B_S\) as exhaustion of \(N_S\) soft trials without acceptance and \(B_R\) as exhaustion of \(N_R\) full-restoration trials, repeated model inconsistency, or failure to obtain positive predicted violation reduction. The escalation rule is \[S_k\xrightarrow{B_S}R_k,\qquad R_k\xrightarrow{B_R}E_k.\] Emergency failure produces a declared terminal restoration status. Escalation never discards the last accepted iterate, and returning to a less severe mode requires a separately satisfied restoration-return predicate.
assumptions_latex: Each mode distinguishes accepted iterates from rejected trial points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_S\) triggers \(S_k\to R_k\), and \(B_R\) triggers \(R_k\to E_k\), while preserving the last accepted iterate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordered predicates for moving from soft to full and then emergency restoration.

notation.meaning: soft, full, and emergency restoration modes

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: ordered escalation formalizes increasingly severe restoration safeguards

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The condition kind is appropriate for escalation predicates, but the ordered soft-to-full-to-emergency architecture, budgets, triggers, preservation rule, and return restriction are uncited and not universal. The immutable path also repeats the title and supplies no role, so evidence is especially necessary to establish the intended local sense without altering the taxonomy.

children.top_down_role: Frameworks separating approximate feasibility improvement from optimization on restored local geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in X}f(x)\) subject to a constraint mapping \(c(x)\) with violation measure \(V(x)\). At iteration \(k\), let \(x_k\) be the current point, \(y_k\) a restored point, and \(z_k\) an optimization trial point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic methods that compute approximate restoration and optimization steps under separate accuracy and acceptance conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inexact restoration method is an iterative scheme in which each major iteration has two separately controlled tasks. The restoration task computes \(y_k\in X\) satisfying an inexact feasibility condition such as \[V(y_k)\le r_kV(x_k),\qquad 0\le r_k<1,\] or an approximate stationarity condition for \(\min_XV\). The optimization task then computes \(z_k=y_k+t_k\), where \(t_k\) approximately minimizes a local model of \(f\) while remaining on or near the restored local geometry, for example \[\nabla c(y_k)^Tt_k=0\quad\text{or}\quad \|c(y_k)+\nabla c(y_k)^Tt_k\|\le\delta_k.\] The trial point becomes \(x_{k+1}\) only if an independent line-search, trust-region, merit, or filter acceptance test holds. Neither task is required to be solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact restoration method separates each major iteration into an approximate feasibility task and an approximate optimization task. The first produces a restored point with prescribed violation reduction or restoration stationarity. The second improves an objective model along the restored local constraint geometry. An independent globalization test decides whether the resulting trial point becomes the next iterate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining decomposition is \(x_k\mapsto y_k\mapsto z_k\), with separate inexactness tests for restoration and optimization and a separate acceptance test for \(z_k\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: In composite-step terminology, \(y_k=x_k+n_k\) is generated by a normal step and \(z_k=y_k+t_k\) by a tangential step.
special_cases_latex: Line-search inexact restoration globalizes \(t_k\) by a step length.
Trust-region inexact restoration restricts the normal and tangential computations by a radius \(\Delta_k\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Feasibility and optimality accuracies can be varied independently.
The restored point \(y_k\) need not itself become a major iterate.
boundary_notes: The definition does not require exact feasibility of \(y_k\).
A generic composite step is included only when its feasibility and optimization tasks have the stated independent controls.

notation.meaning: Optimization step on restored local geometry.

children.title: Feasibility–Optimality Phase Separation
children.top_down_role: Independent structural control of restoration and objective improvement.

knowledge_statements.title: Restoration-Retention Is Algorithm Dependent
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Phase separation does not automatically mean that a restored point survives rejection of the optimality trial; the iteration's transition rule must say so.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Separate restoration and optimality acceptance predicates do not by themselves determine the next iterate. If an optimality trial \(z_k\) is rejected, retaining \(y_k\), returning to \(x_k\), or invoking another restoration attempt are different valid transition rules. Therefore the implication \[\text{optimality rejection}\Longrightarrow x_{k+1}=y_k\] holds only when it is explicitly included in the restoration algorithm.
assumptions_latex: Restoration and optimality trials are evaluated by distinct predicates.
No next-iterate transition rule is otherwise assumed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Retention of }y_k\text{ after rejecting }z_k\text{ is framework dependent}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary on what phase separation alone implies after optimality-trial rejection.

knowledge_statements.title: Two-Phase Inexact-Restoration Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inexact restoration first seeks a separately tested reduction in constraint violation and then seeks objective improvement on approximate restored geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), let \(v(x)\ge0\) vanish exactly when \(c(x)=0\). A phase-separated inexact-restoration iteration first computes a restored point \(y_k\) using a feasibility model or oracle and requires a declared reduction test for \(v\). It then computes an optimality trial \(z_k\) from \(y_k\) using an objective or Lagrangian model restricted to approximate restored constraint geometry. The restoration and optimality trials have distinct predicted-reduction and acceptance predicates, so feasibility progress and objective progress are assessed as separate algorithmic quantities.
assumptions_latex: A violation measure \(v\) is specified with \(v(x)=0\iff c(x)=0\).
The algorithm specifies separate feasibility and optimality models and acceptance predicates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Restoration acceptance and optimality acceptance are distinct parts of the iteration interface}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Family-defining separation of feasibility restoration from objective improvement.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V:X\to\mathbb R_+\) measure constraint violation and let \(m_k^f\) be a local objective model. A major iteration starts at \(x_k\), produces a restored point \(y_k\), and may produce an optimization trial \(z_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural definition for finite-dimensional restoration and composite-step methods; it concerns control separation rather than temporal separation into unrelated algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A method has feasibility–optimality phase separation when its restoration and optimization tasks are defined by distinct mathematical conditions: \[y_k\in\mathcal F_k:=\{y\in X:V(y)\le r_kV(x_k)\}\] or an explicitly stated approximate-stationarity substitute, followed by \[z_k\in\mathcal O_k(y_k):=\{y_k+t:t\in T_k(y_k),\ m_k^f(y_k+t)\le m_k^f(y_k)-\delta_k\}.\] Here \(r_k<1\), \(\delta_k\ge0\), and \(T_k(y_k)\) approximates the tangent geometry of the restored constraints. The feasibility task is judged without requiring objective decrease, while the optimization task is judged by objective-model progress subject to preservation, within tolerance, of the restored geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility–optimality phase separation means that restoration and objective improvement have different feasible sets, tolerances, and success tests. The first phase seeks prescribed reduction or stationarity of constraint violation without requiring objective decrease. The second seeks objective-model decrease along an approximation of the restored constraint geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sets \(\mathcal F_k\) and \(\mathcal O_k(y_k)\) are controlled independently, so feasibility success does not imply optimality success and conversely.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In normal–tangential terminology, the normal step controls feasibility and the tangential step controls objective-model reduction.
special_cases_latex: If \(T_k(y_k)=\ker\nabla c(y_k)^T\), the optimization phase preserves linearized equalities exactly.
If no satisfactory optimization step exists, the algorithm may accept \(y_k\) as a feasibility-only outcome when its outer rules permit.
immediate_consequences_latex: Restoration accuracy may be relaxed without changing the optimization model-decrease threshold.
Failure of the optimization phase does not invalidate an already achieved restoration reduction.
boundary_notes: A single scalar merit function does not exhibit this separation unless its algorithm still maintains distinct phase conditions.
The definition does not require exact tangency or exact restoration.

notation.meaning: Set of points satisfying the kth feasibility-phase requirement.
Set of acceptable optimization trials based at the restored point.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility–Optimality Phase Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural principle for equality-constrained inexact restoration methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \\(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\\) subject to \\(c(x)=0\\), with violation measure \\(v(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\\). At iteration \\(k\\), a restoration phase computes \\(y_k\\) using only a model or oracle for \\(v\\) and requires \\(v(y_k)\le v(x_k)-\delta_k\\) for some \\(\delta_k>0\\). An optimality phase then computes a trial point \\(z_k\\) from \\(y_k\\) using a model of \\(f\\) restricted to an approximate tangent space of the constraints. Acceptance tests for restoration and optimality are evaluated independently; failure of the optimality test may reject \\(z_k\\) without invalidating the achieved restoration at \\(y_k\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration first reduces constraint violation; a separate tangential phase seeks objective improvement. Rejecting the optimality trial does not erase an independently accepted feasibility improvement.
assumptions_latex: \\(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\\) and \\(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\\) are continuously differentiable.
The restoration and optimality phases have separately specified acceptance tests.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility restoration and objective improvement can be controlled and accepted independently.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle fits the terminal container, but independent acceptance and retention of the restored point are framework-specific features rather than consequences of the stated smoothness assumptions. A restoration-method source with a precise algorithm or section locator is required.

children.title: Tangential Optimization after Restoration
children.top_down_role: Optimality improvement on an approximation of restored constraint geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Form of the Tangential Subproblem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal tangent-space basis converts the post-restoration tangential problem into a norm-preserving reduced trust-region problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J_k=\nabla c(y_k)\), and let the columns of \(Z_k\) form an orthonormal basis of \(\ker J_k\). Every exactly tangential step has the form \(t=Z_kp\), and \[\min_{J_kt=0,\ \|t\|\le\Delta_k} g_k^\top t+\tfrac12t^\top B_kt\] is equivalent to \[\min_{\|p\|\le\Delta_k}(Z_k^\top g_k)^\top p+\tfrac12p^\top(Z_k^\top B_kZ_k)p.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tangential feasibility, model values, and the Euclidean radius are preserved under \(t=Z_kp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduced-coordinate representation of post-restoration tangential optimization.

notation.meaning: Orthonormal basis of the restored linearized tangent space.
Objective gradient at the restored point.

knowledge_statements.title: Tangential Optimization after Restoration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-constrained tangential correction following a restored point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a restored point \(y_k\), gradient \(g_k=\nabla f(y_k)\), constraint Jacobian \(J_k=J_c(y_k)\), symmetric matrix \(B_k\), and radius \(\Delta_k>0\), compute
\[
t_k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{J_kt=0,\ \|t\|\le\Delta_k}\; g_k^Tt+\tfrac12t^TB_kt.
\]
Set the trial point to \(z_k=y_k+t_k\), evaluate its nonlinear objective and constraints, and accept it only under the method's coupled optimality-feasibility globalization test. The equation \(J_kt_k=0\) preserves the linearized equality-constraint model at \(y_k\); it does not guarantee \(c(z_k)=c(y_k)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After restoration, minimize a quadratic objective model in the Jacobian null space, then test the corrected point for actual objective and feasibility behavior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The computed correction satisfies \(J_c(y_k)t_k=0\), so it leaves the linearized equality constraints unchanged.

notation.meaning: constraint Jacobian at the restored point

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tangential optimization subproblem at a restored point
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For equality constraints \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\), let \(y_k=x_k+n_k\) be a restored point, \(J_k=\nabla c(y_k)^T\), and \(m_k^f(t)=f(y_k)+g_k^Tt+\tfrac12t^TB_kt\) an objective model.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equality-constrained form; active inequalities may be appended to the tangent model through an active-set or cone condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Tangential optimization after restoration is the computation of an approximate solution \(t_k\) of \[\min_t\ m_k^f(t)\quad\text{subject to}\quad J_kt=0,\quad y_k+t\in X,\quad \|n_k+t\|\le\Delta_k,\] or of an inexact variant satisfying \(\|J_kt\|\le\delta_k\). The trial point is \(z_k=y_k+t_k\). A nonzero tangential step must achieve a declared model decrease, for example \[m_k^f(0)-m_k^f(t_k)\ge\kappa\chi_k\min\{\chi_k/\beta_k,\Delta_k\},\] where \(\chi_k\) is a tangential first-order criticality measure. The tangency condition prevents first-order destruction of the restored equality geometry while the model-decrease condition targets optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After restoration, tangential optimization approximately minimizes a local objective model over directions tangent, or nearly tangent, to the restored constraint geometry. The combined trial point is the restored point plus the tangential step. A prescribed model-decrease condition measures optimality progress, while the tangency tolerance limits first-order loss of restored feasibility.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining conditions are objective-model decrease and \(J_kt=0\) or \(\|J_kt\|\le\delta_k\) at the restored point.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With a null-space basis \(Z_k\) satisfying \(J_kZ_k=0\), write \(t=Z_kw\) and minimize the reduced model over \(w\).
special_cases_latex: If \(y_k\) is exactly feasible and \(J_kt_k=0\), the equality residual changes only beyond its linear term.
For active inequalities, \(t_k\) may be restricted to a linearized tangent cone rather than a null space.
immediate_consequences_latex: The tangential task can be omitted when \(\chi_k\) already meets its optimality tolerance.
Restoration and tangential steps may use different accuracy requirements.
boundary_notes: Tangency preserves feasibility only to first order for nonlinear constraints.
The definition does not require \(B_k\) to be positive definite if the local subproblem remains well posed.

children.title: Line-Search Inexact Restoration
children.top_down_role: Inexact restoration coupled to step-length globalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Armijo Backtracking for Restoration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous differentiability and strict violation descent ensure that a sufficiently short restoration step satisfies the Armijo test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) be continuously differentiable near \(x_k\), let \(\nabla v(x_k)^\top d_k<0\), and choose \(\beta,\sigma\in(0,1)\). Then there exists \(j<\infty\) such that \(\alpha_j=\beta^j\) satisfies \[v(x_k+\alpha_jd_k)\le v(x_k)+\sigma\alpha_j\nabla v(x_k)^\top d_k.\] Thus the mathematical Armijo backtracking sequence accepts after finitely many reductions; an implementation may instead report failure only if an external step or evaluation safeguard intervenes first.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists j<\infty:\ v(x_k+\beta^jd_k)\le v(x_k)+\sigma\beta^j\nabla v(x_k)^\top d_k.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-definedness of restoration backtracking along a strict violation-descent direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Search Inexact Restoration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Backtrack along an inexact feasibility-descent direction until an Armijo decrease in constraint violation is obtained, then pass the restored point to the optimality phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \\(x_k\\), compute an inexact restoration direction \\(d_k\\) satisfying \\(\nabla v(x_k)^\top d_k<0\\), where \\(v(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\\). Initialize \\(\alpha=1\\) and choose constants \\(\beta\in(0,1)\\) and \\(\sigma\in(0,1)\\). While \\[v(x_k+\alpha d_k)>v(x_k)+\sigma\alpha\nabla v(x_k)^\top d_k,\] replace \\(\alpha\\) by \\(\beta\alpha\\). Output \\(y_k=x_k+\alpha d_k\\) when the inequality is reversed. A subsequent optimality trial is subjected to its own line search or coupled acceptance test; restoration is declared unsuccessful if the prescribed minimum step length or evaluation budget is reached first.
assumptions_latex: An inexact direction with strict descent for \\(v\\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any accepted step satisfies a quantified decrease in the restoration merit \\(v\\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Step-length globalization of an inexact restoration trial.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Line-search globalization of an inexact restoration trial
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(y_k\) satisfy an inexact restoration condition, let \(d_k\) be an optimization direction computed from \(y_k\), and define \(z_k(\alpha)=y_k+\alpha d_k\) for \(\alpha\in(0,1]\). Let \(A_k(z)\) be the outer acceptance predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic inexact-restoration methods whose optimization trial is globalized by backtracking along a direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A line-search inexact restoration iteration computes \(y_k\) with \(V(y_k)\le r_kV(x_k)\), chooses an optimization direction \(d_k\), and selects \[\alpha_k=\max\{\beta^j:j\in\mathbb N_0,\ A_k(y_k+\beta^jd_k)\},\qquad \beta\in(0,1).\] The acceptance predicate must impose declared sufficient progress, for example a merit decrease or filter margin, and may include a restoration-preservation condition \[V(y_k+\alpha d_k)\le V(y_k)+\tau_k.\] If no acceptable scale satisfies \(\alpha\ge\alpha_{\min}\), the iteration rejects the optimization trial and invokes the specified restoration-entry, restoration-return, or failure rule. Thus restoration accuracy and line-search acceptance are separate tests.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Line-search inexact restoration first computes an approximately restored point and an optimization direction. It then backtracks over geometrically decreasing step lengths until the trial satisfies the outer merit or filter condition and any permitted loss-of-feasibility bound. If no acceptable step remains above the minimum scale, the optimization trial is rejected and the method follows its restoration or failure rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The accepted major iterate is \(x_{k+1}=y_k+\alpha_kd_k\), where \(\alpha_k\) is selected by a declared backtracking acceptance predicate independent of the restoration test.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The line search can be written as the first \(j\ge0\) for which \(A_k(y_k+\beta^jd_k)\) holds.
special_cases_latex: For a filter, \(A_k\) requires the trial pair \((V,f)\) to satisfy a sufficient margin relative to every filter entry.
A feasibility-only return accepts \(y_k\) without a nonzero optimization step when the architecture permits it.
immediate_consequences_latex: A successful restoration does not guarantee acceptance of the full optimization step.
Backtracking changes the optimization displacement while leaving the restored base point fixed.
boundary_notes: The definition does not prescribe Wolfe conditions, which need not suit nonsmooth filter acceptance.
A step length below \(\alpha_{\min}\) is an algorithmic failure trigger, not an infeasibility certificate.

children.title: Trust-Region Inexact Restoration
children.top_down_role: Inexact restoration coupled to restricted local models.

knowledge_statements.title: Fraction-of-Cauchy Restoration Decrease
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inexact restoration step is adequate when it obtains a uniform Cauchy-type decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m_k(s)=m_k(0)+g_k^\top s+\tfrac12s^\top H_ks\), an admissible step \(s_k\) is adequately solved if \[m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)\ge\kappa_{\mathrm{fcd}}\|g_k\|\min\!\left\{\Delta_k,\frac{\|g_k\|}{1+\|H_k\|}\right\},\] where \(\kappa_{\mathrm{fcd}}>0\) is independent of \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The predicted restoration decrease is positive whenever \(g_k\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient quality certificate for an inexact restoration trust-region step.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Restoration Stationarity under Trust-Region Acceptance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under standard trust-region smoothness, model, decrease, and radius safeguards, an infinite restoration run drives the violation gradient to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v\) be bounded below and continuously differentiable with Lipschitz gradient on a neighborhood of the restoration iterates. Suppose the quadratic models have gradient \(\nabla v(x_k)\), uniformly bounded curvature, the trial steps satisfy a uniform fraction-of-Cauchy decrease, and standard ratio-acceptance and radius-update safeguards are used. Then every infinite restoration sequence satisfies \[\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla v(x_k)\|=0.\]
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is bounded below on the relevant level set.
\(\nabla v\) is Lipschitz near the iterates.
Trial steps satisfy a uniform fraction-of-Cauchy decrease.
The standard trust-region radius safeguards are enforced.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{k\to\infty}\|\nabla v(x_k)\|=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order global convergence of an infinite restoration phase.

knowledge_statements.title: Trust-Region Inexact Restoration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximately minimize a local violation model inside a radius, accept according to actual-to-predicted reduction, and update the radius using the agreement ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \\(x_k\\), build a local model \\(m_k(s)\\) of the violation measure \\(v(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\\). Compute an approximate step \\(s_k\\) satisfying \\(\|s_k\|\le\Delta_k\\) and \\(m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)>0\\). Evaluate \\[\rho_k=\frac{v(x_k)-v(x_k+s_k)}{m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)}.\] If \\(\rho_k\ge\eta_1\\), accept \\(y_k=x_k+s_k\\); otherwise set \\(y_k=x_k\\). Shrink \\(\Delta_k\\) when \\(\rho_k<\eta_1\\), permit enlargement when \\(\rho_k\ge\eta_2\\) and \\(\|s_k\|\\) is near \\(\Delta_k\\), where \\(0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1\\). Stop when feasibility or restoration-stationarity tolerance is met.
assumptions_latex: The model decrease is positive for every ratio test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Accepted restoration steps have positive actual violation reduction, while poor model agreement contracts the region.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trust-region globalization of a local constraint-violation model.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At iteration \(k\), let \(n_k\) be an approximate restoration step, \(t_k\) an approximate tangential step, \(s_k=n_k+t_k\), and \(\Delta_k>0\) the trust-region radius. Let \(m_k^V\) and \(m_k^f\) model violation and objective behavior.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A trust-region inexact restoration iteration computes \(n_k\) and \(t_k\) subject to \[\|n_k\|\le\kappa_\Delta\Delta_k,\qquad \|n_k+t_k\|\le\Delta_k,\qquad 0<\kappa_\Delta\le1,\] where \(n_k\) attains a prescribed fraction of achievable decrease in \(m_k^V\), and \(t_k\) attains a prescribed decrease in \(m_k^f\) while satisfying the restored linearized geometry. The trial \(x_k+s_k\) is accepted only if its actual feasibility and objective behavior is adequate relative to the predicted behavior, as measured by declared ratio or filter tests. Rejection leaves \(x_k\) unchanged and reduces \(\Delta_k\); incompatibility of the restricted local problem invokes restoration or escalation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Trust-region inexact restoration restricts both the feasibility-improving step and the combined feasibility–optimality step to a neighborhood of the current iterate. Each component need only meet a quantitative approximate-decrease condition. The combined trial is accepted by actual-versus-predicted or filter tests; rejection contracts the radius, while incompatibility invokes restoration or escalation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The defining local restriction is \(\|n_k+t_k\|\le\Delta_k\), with separately quantified approximate feasibility and objective-model decreases and an outer acceptance test.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The method may first compute \(y_k=x_k+n_k\) and then solve a tangential trust-region subproblem based at \(y_k\).
special_cases_latex: A normal-step compatibility test may require \(\|n_k\|\le\kappa_\Delta\Delta_k\min\{1,\kappa_\mu\Delta_k^\mu\}\).
Filter-SQP accepts a trial through feasibility or objective progress without a penalty parameter.

An incompatible normal step can trigger restoration before a tangential step is attempted.

The definition permits approximate rather than exact trust-region subproblem solutions.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let a restoration run start from \(x_k\), produce a terminal point \(y\in X\), use violation measure \(V\), stationarity residual \(\sigma_V(y)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial V(y)+N_X(y))\), and count work \(W\). Fix tolerances \(\varepsilon_V,\varepsilon_S\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional deterministic restoration outcomes. Certificates are algorithmic and local unless explicitly strengthened by convexity or dual information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration outcome-certificate system is a mutually distinguished set of terminal labels with quantitative predicates. The canonical labels are \[\mathsf{SUCCESS}:\quad V(y)\le\varepsilon_V\ \text{and the return-compatibility test holds},\] \[\mathsf{STATIONARY\_VIOLATION}:\quad \sigma_V(y)\le\varepsilon_S,\] \[\mathsf{LOCAL\_INFEASIBILITY\_INDICATION}:\quad V(y)>\varepsilon_V\ \text{and}\ \sigma_V(y)\le\varepsilon_S,\] and \[\mathsf{WORK\_LIMIT}:\quad W\ge W_{\max}\ \text{before another terminal predicate holds}.\] The emitted record includes \((V(y),\sigma_V(y),W)\), the tolerances, and the restoration model used. The local-infeasibility label is an indication, not a proof that the original global feasible set is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A restoration outcome-certificate system assigns a terminal label using explicit residuals and tolerances. Success requires small violation and compatibility with renewed optimization. Stationary violation requires a small first-order residual for the violation problem. Positive violation together with that stationarity residual is a local infeasibility indication. Exhausting the declared work budget is a separate outcome.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every terminal restoration run is classified by declared predicates involving \(V(y)\), \(\sigma_V(y)\), compatibility, and work, rather than by an unqualified success or failure message.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For smooth least-squares violation \(V(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|_2^2\) and unconstrained \(X\), \(\sigma_V(y)=\|J_c(y)^Tc(y)\|\).
special_cases_latex: Exact restoration success uses \(\varepsilon_V=0\).
A complexity-aware implementation reports function, derivative, and subproblem evaluations as separate components of \(W\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A work-limit outcome makes no stationarity or infeasibility assertion unless another predicate also holds.
The numerical values accompanying a label permit tolerance-dependent reinterpretation.
boundary_notes: Positive stationary violation is only local evidence in a nonconvex problem.
A rigorous global infeasibility certificate requires additional structure not included here.

knowledge_statements.title: Successful Restoration Outcomes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration succeeds when the returned point is sufficiently feasible or achieves the required relative violation reduction and also satisfies the next phase's entry conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(x_k\\) be the point that triggered restoration and let \\(y_k\\) be its output. Given tolerances \\(\varepsilon_c\ge0\\) and \\(\kappa_v\in(0,1)\\), a successful-restoration certificate is the pair of verified inequalities \\[\|c(y_k)\|\le\varepsilon_c\qquad\text{or}\qquad \|c(y_k)\|\le\kappa_v\|c(x_k)\|,\] together with satisfaction of every domain, bound, or model-validity condition required by the next optimality phase. If the disjunction and the phase-entry conditions hold, \\(y_k\\) is certified suitable for renewed optimality processing; the certificate alone does not assert stationarity or optimality of \\(y_k\\).
assumptions_latex: Constraint residuals at \\(x_k\\) and \\(y_k\\) can be evaluated to the certification accuracy.
The optimality phase has explicit entry conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed checks certify eligibility to leave restoration, but not optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Computable certificate for returning from restoration to optimality iterations.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is the appropriate mathematical role, but the disjunctive absolute-or-relative success rule and phase-entry conditions are method-dependent and are not supported by a citation. A source defining this restoration success certificate is required.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let restoration begin at \(x_k\) and return a candidate \(y_k\in X\). Let \(V\) be the violation measure, \(\varepsilon_k\ge0\) an absolute tolerance, \(r_k\in[0,1)\) a relative reduction factor, and \(C_k(y)\) the ordinary-mode compatibility predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithmic success for finite-dimensional restoration phases; success means suitability for renewed optimization, not optimality of the original nonlinear program.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A successful restoration outcome is a returned point \(y_k\) satisfying \[V(y_k)\le\max\{\varepsilon_k,r_kV(x_k)\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad C_k(y_k)=\mathrm{true}.\] The compatibility predicate may state that \(y_k\) is acceptable to the current filter, that a local constrained step-generation problem at \(y_k\) is compatible for some positive radius, or that another declared ordinary-mode acceptance condition holds. The success certificate records \(x_k,y_k,V(x_k),V(y_k),\varepsilon_k,r_k\), and the satisfied compatibility test. It authorizes a transition from restoration to ordinary optimization but does not assert first-order optimality of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restoration succeeds when the returned point has sufficiently small absolute or relative constraint violation and also satisfies the compatibility condition needed by the ordinary optimization mechanism. The recorded certificate identifies the reduction and the compatibility test. Success authorizes renewed optimization; it does not declare the point optimal.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The success predicate is the conjunction of quantitative feasibility recovery and ordinary-mode compatibility.
equivalent_formulations_latex: A purely absolute success test is obtained with \(r_k=0\).
A purely relative recovery test is \(V(y_k)\le r_kV(x_k)\), supplemented by compatibility.
special_cases_latex: For filter methods, compatibility means sufficient filter acceptability.
For trust-region SQP, compatibility may mean existence of a normal step leaving adequate radius for tangential progress.
immediate_consequences_latex: Small violation alone need not authorize return if the ordinary local model remains incompatible.
A successful returned point may still be infeasible when \(\varepsilon_k>0\).
boundary_notes: Restoration success is distinct from convergence of the original nonlinear program.
The relative test is ineffective when no strict factor \(r_k<1\) is prescribed.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Violation Stationarity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order restoration stationarity combines the normal-equation residual with positive semidefiniteness of the exact violation Hessian; negative curvature rejects local minimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(c\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(v(x)=	frac12\|c(x)\|^2\), then \[
abla^2v(y)=J_c(y)^	op J_c(y)+\sum_{i=1}^m c_i(y)
abla^2c_i(y).\] A local minimizer of \(v\) necessarily satisfies \(J_c(y)^	op c(y)=0\) and \(
abla^2v(y)\succeq0\). A stationary point with \(d^	op
abla^2v(y)d<0\) for some \(d\) is not a local violation minimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local violation minimality implies \(J_c(y)^\top c(y)=0\) and \(\nabla^2v(y)\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order outcome test for equality-only squared-residual restoration.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be closed and let \(V:X\to\mathbb R_+\) be a locally Lipschitz constraint-violation measure. Let \(\partial V(x)\) denote a specified generalized subdifferential and \(N_X(x)\) the corresponding normal cone.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationary outcomes for smooth or nonsmooth finite-dimensional violation minimization; no convexity is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A point \(\bar x\in X\) is a stationary constraint-violation outcome when \[0\in\partial V(\bar x)+N_X(\bar x).\] An \(\varepsilon\)-stationary outcome satisfies \[\operatorname{dist}\bigl(0,\partial V(\bar x)+N_X(\bar x)\bigr)\le\varepsilon.\] For the smooth least-squares measure \(V(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|_2^2\) on \(X=\mathbb R^n\), this becomes \[\|J_c(\bar x)^Tc(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon.\] The outcome certificate records both \(V(\bar x)\) and its stationarity residual: \(V(\bar x)=0\) is a stationary feasible outcome, while \(V(\bar x)>0\) is a stationary positive-violation outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stationary constraint-violation outcome is a point satisfying the first-order stationarity condition for minimizing the selected violation measure over the restoration domain. Approximate stationarity is defined by the distance of zero from the subdifferential plus the domain normal cone. The certificate must also report the violation value, because stationary feasible and stationary positive-violation outcomes have different meanings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stationarity is measured for the auxiliary problem \(\min_{x\in X}V(x)\), independently of stationarity for the original objective.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For unconstrained smooth \(V\), the condition is \(\|\nabla V(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
For least-squares violation, it is \(\|J_c(\bar x)^Tc(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon\).
special_cases_latex: If \(V(\bar x)=0\), the point is feasible regardless of whether it is stationary for the original objective.
If \(V(\bar x)>0\), the point is locally stationary for violation but not feasible.
immediate_consequences_latex: A restoration algorithm may terminate meaningfully without finding feasibility.
Changing the violation norm changes the stationarity condition and potentially the reported point.
boundary_notes: First-order stationarity does not imply local minimality for a nonconvex violation function.
Positive stationary violation does not alone prove that the global feasible set is empty.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity certificate for equality-constraint restoration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For continuously differentiable \\(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\\), define \\(v(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\\). Given \\(\varepsilon_s\ge0\\), a point \\(y\\) has an \\(\varepsilon_s\\)-stationary constraint-violation certificate when \\[\|\nabla v(y)\|=\|J_c(y)^\top c(y)\|\le\varepsilon_s.\] For \\(\varepsilon_s=0\\), this is exact first-order stationarity of the unconstrained restoration problem \\(\min_x v(x)\\). If additionally \\(\|c(y)\|>0\\), the outcome is stationary but infeasible for the original equality constraints; it does not by itself prove that no feasible point exists nearby or globally.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A small transposed-Jacobian residual certifies approximate stationarity of squared constraint violation. Positive constraint residual means stationary infeasibility, not a proof that the original problem is infeasible.

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz Neighborhood Exclusion Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual larger than its maximum Lipschitz variation across a ball certifies that the ball contains no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c\) be \(L_c\)-Lipschitz on \(B(y,r)\). If \(\|c(y)\|>L_cr\), then every \(x\in B(y,r)\) satisfies \[\|c(x)\|\ge \|c(y)\|-L_c\|x-y\|>0.\] Hence \(c(x)=0\) has no solution in \(B(y,r)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: B(y,r)\cap\{x:c(x)=0\}=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative local infeasibility indication from a positive residual and a local Lipschitz bound.

notation.meaning: Closed radius-r neighborhood of the restoration outcome.
Certified local Lipschitz constant of the residual map.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(V:X\to\mathbb R_+\) be the restoration violation measure, with \(V(x)=0\) exactly for feasible \(x\). Let \(\sigma_V(x)=\operatorname{dist}(0,\partial V(x)+N_X(x))\), and fix \(\varepsilon_V>0\) and \(\varepsilon_S\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local, first-order diagnostic for finite-dimensional nonconvex constraint systems; it is deliberately weaker than a global infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A restoration point \(\bar x\in X\) provides an \((\varepsilon_V,\varepsilon_S)\)-local infeasibility indication when \[V(\bar x)>\varepsilon_V\qquad\text{and}\qquad \sigma_V(\bar x)\le\varepsilon_S.\] Thus the constraints remain materially violated while the chosen violation problem is approximately first-order stationary. In the smooth least-squares case \(V(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|_2^2\) and \(X=\mathbb R^n\), the diagnostic is \[\tfrac12\|c(\bar x)\|_2^2>\varepsilon_V,\qquad \|J_c(\bar x)^Tc(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon_S.\] The certificate must name \(V\), its domain, both tolerances, and the final residuals. Its assertion is limited to the selected restoration model and the region reached by the restoration run.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A local infeasibility indication occurs when restoration stops at a point with materially positive constraint violation but a small first-order stationarity residual for the violation-minimization problem. It indicates that local first-order restoration cannot readily reduce the selected violation measure. It does not certify that no feasible point exists elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive residual plus approximate stationarity of \(V\) constitutes local incompatibility evidence, not global infeasibility.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For smooth unconstrained violation minimization, use \(V(\bar x)>\varepsilon_V\) and \(\|\nabla V(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon_S\).
For least squares, use \(\|c(\bar x)\|>\sqrt{2\varepsilon_V}\) and \(\|J_c(\bar x)^Tc(\bar x)\|\le\varepsilon_S\).
special_cases_latex: If \(V\) is convex on a convex domain and stationarity is exact, a positive global minimum establishes infeasibility within that modeled domain; this is stronger than the general local indication.
For a linear elastic restoration problem solved globally, a positive optimum certifies inconsistency of that linearized system within its domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: The diagnostic distinguishes stagnation at positive violation from successful restoration.
Restarting from a different region or changing the violation measure may yield a different outcome.
boundary_notes: Nonconvex stationarity neither proves local minimality nor global infeasibility.
A positive residual without a stationarity residual is only failed progress, not this certificate.

notation.meaning: Stationarity residual for the violation problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Local Infeasibility Indications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of positive-residual restoration-stationarity evidence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \\(v(x)=\tfrac12\|c(x)\|^2\\). An exact outcome satisfying \\(J_c(y)^\top c(y)=0\\) and \\(c(y)\ne0\\) certifies only that \\(y\\) is a stationary infeasible point of \\(v\\). It is not a local-infeasibility certificate without additional curvature and isolation conditions. Indeed, for \\(c(x)=x^2-1\\), the point \\(y=0\\) satisfies \\(c(0)=-1\\) and \\(c'(0)c(0)=0\\), although feasible points \\(x=\pm1\\) exist. A genuine local indication may be obtained if \\(y\\) is a strict local minimizer of \\(v\\) with \\(v(y)>0\\), because then some neighborhood of \\(y\\) contains no zero of \\(c\\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive-residual stationarity alone does not establish infeasibility. Strict local minimality of violation at a positive value excludes feasible points only in a neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: Local infeasibility means absence of a zero of \\(c\\) in some neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Stationarity with positive residual is merely indicative; strict positive local minimality is sufficient for neighborhood-level infeasibility.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure boundary is the correct kind, and both the counterexample and the distinction between positive-residual stationarity and strict positive local minimality are mathematically sound. knowledge_statements.title: Order-p Regularized Restoration Bound for First-Order Criticality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Order-p regularization reaches first-order restoration stationarity in order epsilon to the negative (p+1)/p evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\ge1\), let \(v\) be bounded below, and suppose \(\nabla^p v\) is Lipschitz on the relevant level set. An adaptive order-\(p\) regularization method satisfying its standard model, subproblem-accuracy, and acceptance conditions reaches \(\|\nabla v(x)\|\le\varepsilon\) in \[O\!\left(\varepsilon^{-(p+1)/p}\right)\] evaluations of \(v\) and its derivatives through order \(p\).
assumptions_latex: \(v\) is bounded below on the generated level set.
\(\nabla^p v\) is Lipschitz on that set.
Models, subproblem solutions, and acceptance tests satisfy the adaptive-regularization accuracy conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{p,1}(\varepsilon)=O\!\left(\varepsilon^{-(p+1)/p}\right).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Higher-derivative evaluation family targeting first-order stationarity of a smooth restoration objective.

notation.meaning: Highest derivative order used by the regularized restoration model.

abla v(x_k)\|>\varepsilon\) guarantees \[v(x_k)-v(x_{k+1})\ge\kappa\|
abla v(x_k)\|^2\] with \(\kappa>0\), then at most \[\left\lceil rac{v(x_0)-v_{\inf}}{\kappa\varepsilon^2}ightceil=O(\varepsilon^{-2})\] successful iterations occur before \(\|
abla v\|\le\varepsilon\). The same evaluation order follows only when the declared oracle accounting controls unsuccessful trials proportionally.

Let v be bounded below on the generated level set, suppose
